speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Under the government's high employment program a reconstruction fund was set aside to take care of spotty unemployment in certain areas. If a serious unemployment situation developed, funds could be allocated to various departments of the government in .order to proceed with needed public works in the area. As employment has been high, it has been used only to a limited extent.
To what extent?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There was a survey of the St. Lawrence waterway project, $63,000; a survey of the Red Deer river project, $107,000; a survey of the South river project, $120^000; reconditioning and altering .of M.V. Huascaran, now the S.S. Beaverbrae, for the .carriage of immigrants, $300,000. The actual expendFtures last year under this vote were $591,419.21.

The minister stated that the purpose of this vote is to develop projects in sections of the country where employment may be spotty, but he went on to say that in view of the high level of employment across the country it has not been necessary to use it, I notice that the surveys that were made were in Ontario and the west.
{Mr. Howe.]
I cannot accept the minister's statement that there is a high level of employment in all parts of the country, because that certainly is not true in the maritimes. It is evident that the maritime provinces have been neglected completely as far as expenditures under this vote are concerned. The committee of reconstruction of this house functioned in 1942 and 1943 and brought in a comprehensive report dealing with projects that it regarded as necessary in the aftermath of the war in order to keep a high level of employment. That committee recommended the carrying out of one project in Nova Scotia having to do with the strait of Canso. That recommendation was accepted, and I am wondering why a survey has not been made.
This matter has been passed on to the Department of Transport, and yet this particular vote is provided to relieve any unemployment situation that might exist. I expect to see very little done by the department which now has the matter under consideration. I submit that if this vote is used for the purpose for which it was intended, this particular matter should receive serious consideration by the department of reconstruction.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: A survey of the strait of Canso has been made, and studies have been prepared of three alternative solutions of the transportation problem. However, it seems to be impossible to obtain agreement between the government and the local and provincial authorities as to a solution that will be acceptable to all parties. The project is in good hands as far as this government is concerned. At the moment there is a commission sitting on it made up of three engineers, one appointed by the province and two by the federal government. I dare say this commission will throw' new light on the subject and great things wall result.

I do not think there is any disagreement as far as the provincial and local authorities are concerned. They are unanimous that the job should be done. The difficulty is with the engineering department of the federal government. I think one of the main difficulties which developed in connection with the project was the tying-in of the realignment of the railroad from that point to New Glasgow. That would add terrifically to the cost. I ask the minister, who is an engineer, to give the matter consideration, and to separate the tunnel, causeway or bridge from the railway project; it would then come within the terms of this vote.
I think the reason for the attitude of the Department of Transport is that railway

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
realignment was tied in with the bridge or causeway or tunnel project across the strait of Canso. I strongly urge upon the minister that he consider the bridge project separately under this vote. He himself has already said that the purpose of the vote is to relieve unemployment in certain areas where it is spotty. Department of Labour statistics show that in the last three years four thousand people have been moved out of Nova Scotia alone to relieve its unemployment situation. Personally I think that bad policy. The people of Nova Scotia today are more or less in the category of displaced persons. Instead of moving the unemployed from Nova Scotia, an endeavour should be made to find employment for them there and to develop this country from coast to coast. It is hard for me to understand the necessity for bringing in a large number of displaced persons from Europe so long as there is unemployment in a large area of Canada. The policy is all to the good from a humanitarian point of view, but it requires re-examination from the point of view of unemployment of our own Canadian people.
I again ask the minister to consider separating the bridge project from the realignment of the railways, because they do not really go together, and see whether the Department of Reconstruction cannot co-operate with the Department of Transport on the bridge project. It would go a long way towards relieving unemployment in that part of the country, and would demonstrate to the people of Nova Scotia that at least one section of the government is thinking in terms of something east of Montreal. In the maritimes the people are acquiring a complex that in the eyes of the government the area east of Montreal is not Canada. Once in a while mention will be made of Halifax and the national harbours board, but there is a stretch of territory three hundred and sixty-five miles long east of Halifax that seems to be ignored by this government. I sometimes wonder when we are discussing national questions in this house whether members know their geography and realize that there are sections of Canada whose people are entitled to consideration from the government other than in the matter of paying taxes.
This is a reconstruction post-war project. I speak of it now because the purpose of this vote is to relieve unemployment. This project was recommended to the house and approved. I do not think much more information can be gained than is now available in the large return that was tabled the other day. It contained report after report by engineers, letter after letter between departments of government, the opinions of coal company engineers and of
government engineers. The feasibility of the project and the necessity for it have never been questioned. The only thing about which there was a difference of opinion was the cost, and I do not think that should be considered at all in a project of this kind. In building such a structure you are creating new work and doing something for coming generations.
If the pioneers of this country who built the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways had thought just in terms of money, had allowed money to be the dominant factor, we would still be without railways. We still pour millions of dollars into the C.N.R. because that railway is a national necessity, and this bridge project should be looked upon in the same light. Money is only a medium of exchange to be used to get things done. The government should go ahead in co-operation with the provincial government and spend some of the taxpayers' money in creating new wealth in this country by proceeding with this bridge project, which coming generations could look at and say: The government in office at that time certainly recognized when they built these improved facilities that there were generations still to come. As it is now, we are using the same old equipment that we had seventy-five years ago, and the government is spending another five or six million dollars in perpetuating that antiquated equipment. It is a waste of money.
I think the minister knows that the island of Cape Breton produces one-third of Canada's basic steel, and it has to be shipped across that strait, which proved to be a bottleneck during the war. When the St. Lawrence river was partly closed because of enemy submarines, equipment had to be provided to unload and transport the coal up the St. Lawrence, at a cost very nearly as much as a permanent bridge would cost. That was done because there was an emergency; the war was on. Today I am thinking in terms of linking up that part of the country with the rest of Canada. Even if the bridge or causeway should cost $54,000,000 -which I doubt, and which engineers who have submitted estimates of cost also doubt- we should be building something for ourselves and for future generations. It would create employment and help to develop that part of the country so that people would have an incentive to come there and invest their money.
The one thing that militates against the development of the maritimes is the lack of transportation facilities. This bridge project was recommended unanimously by a committee of this house which was charged with

examining post-war projects that were necessary and of national importance. This is one of them.
When the minister has a responsibility I know there is no ducking of the issue with him. One thing I like about him is that he puts the cards on the table face up, and if he undertook this responsibility and gave an opinion on it based on his own knowledge, I would be quite satisfied to accept it. But I am not satisfied with all the quibbling and manoeuvring and manipulating that has gone on with regard to these surveys and borings since 1901. As one member of the house who has given a lot of thought to the subject and read the reports of the engineers pro and con, I am convinced that the project is feasible. It will not cost too much money, and it is the direct responsibility of the government, and of the minister, under this vote, as a post-war project.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Let me say this. The Minister of Transport brought down an engineering report from the officers of his department. That report contained a recommendation for improving transportation between the mainland and Cape Breton island. It is only because of local protests that that work is not under way today. I suppose that people who are not prepared to invest five cents in the enterprise can bring down suggestions for the next fifty years, and nothing will be done. If the project could be reduced to reasonable proportions, it seems to me we could get on with it and give the island of Cape Breton transportation facilities equal to the requirements of the situation.
Would the minister mind telling us where these local protests come from?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I could tell the hon. member the names of the people who have come to me in delegations, and to the government in delegations, but I do not know that it would improve the situation. They have come from the province and from the locality. Nothing that the government proposes is any good. If that situation could be remedied, perhaps we could get on with the project.
The reason that I press the point, Mr. Chairman, is that I hold in my hand documents which have been sent to me representing the whole opinion of the community.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

They are not insisting on a tunnel, a causeway, or a bridge. They

demand that the project be built in accordance with whatever plans the government may have; that is all. I have read engineering reports in the returns that I have, and the opinions of engineers who are competent. They do not doubt the feasibility of it. I am surprised to think that anybody locally would object to the government going ahead and making a permanent crossing there in accordance with whatever views of it they may have themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: At the moment a commission is sitting on the project. Why? Because it was demanded by the province and by the local interests. I presume that the report of the commission may not satisfy everybody, and someone will demand something else. If the people there would cease making this a political football, and try to get some practical result there, I think they would have no complaint about getting on. Certainly, if I were the responsible minister, so long as the controversy raged I would do just what the government is doing-wait for the opinion to crystallize on some particular method.

I resent the remark of the minister that this is being made a political football. I do not think he intended that, because the reverse is true. I know that every shade of political opinion in Nova Scotia today, particularly on the island of Cape Breton, is organized into a permanent organization known as the Canso Crossing Association. There is no political opinion in that body. They are meeting weekly, and they represent the whole section of the country. They write to me. I know who they are politically, but that does not enter into the picture at all. It is one thing on which the people of that section of the country are solidly united.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The hon. member will agree that the local organization demanded another report from a board of engineers which is now sitting. The hon. member will agree with that?
Yes, for this reason-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is nothing we can do until the last demand is fulfilled and the report is made by the board of engineers.

The reason they demanded that should be well known to the minister. Perhaps he does not know it, because this has not been under his wing. I think it would be further advanced if it were. He would build the bridge.

He will build it before we adjourn if the hon. member is not careful.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
Why did they demand the board of engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Because they did not like the last one, and I am sure that after this report is brought down they will demand another.
First, the board took a whole year to find out how deep the water was, and spent a lot of money on that.
Oh, oh.

The Minister of Transport made a report to the house. They knew how deep the water was in 1901 because the Waddell Hardessy Company made a survey. After the borings were completed the minister reported to the house. His report was to the effect that it was not considered financially feasible. The cost was too high. That report led the people of Nova Scotia and myself to believe that as far as the government was concerned it was out; that the government was not going to touch it. That was further supported by an appropriation in the estimates of the Minister of Transport's department for improvements to the existing facilities costing
So,000,000, plus all the maintenance costs. When I saw the improvements there, and the new ferry, it led me to believe, as it led the people to believe, that the tunnel project or the bridge or the causeway was finished, that it was not going forward. That did not satisfy the people. It did not satisfy me. That is why they demanded a board of competent engineers. I think it came from the Premier of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: They have that.

They have the board of engineers now. What I am suggesting to the minister now is that under this vote he should endeavour to separate the realignment of the railways from the project itself, which would take away that frightening cost, and decide on a permanent crossing, based on that project alone, rather than allow the matter to rest completely with the transport department. I suggest that he exercise his influence on this department and try to have the project come under the vote having to do with reconstruction, relief and employment, which is a necessary project in Nova Scotia. I suggest that he use whatever influence he has to separate the costs. In my opinion what has retarded the whole project has been the hooking up of the realignment of the railways. That is where the Minister of Transport became involved.
I am not going to argue any further with the minister. I know he agrees with me a hundred per cent, but he just cannot say it publicly. I ask him to give it consideration.

I notice that this item includes the cost of survey and engineering work on the Medicine Hat irrigation project and the diversion of the Red Deer river in Alberta, and the South Saskatchewan. Can the minister tell the committee just what is the status of the Red Deer river diversion project? Is it being held back as a project to provide employment in the future, or, on the other hand, is it the intention of the government to go ahead as rapidly as possible just as soon as men and materials are available for the work?
I know that a small project in connection with the larger one is being carried out this year, but it would be dependent upon surface run-off water for irrigation. Unfortunately in that area in the extremely dry years there is very little run-off, with the result that at the very time when water is most needed for irrigation it is not available. We can never expect irrigation in that area to be a success until we can obtain water from the rivers in the extremely dry years. A tremendous loss of wealth is occurring in that area on account of drought. For the past three years the greater part of that area has been under the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme. Although there was a heavy run-off this spring, complaints are already coming in that crops are drying up. The federal government is having to put out large sums of money in that area for prairie farm rehabilitation, and in certain years feed has to be shipped in. This irrigation project would provide feed lots so that the area could be largely self-supporting. In addition it would provide for an additional population of around 30,000 people.
It is generally agreed that this irrigation project would make the area largely self-supporting, thereby relieving the federal government of a large bill of expenses. Is it the intention to proceed with the project as soon as men and materials are available, or is it being held back as one of the relief projects to provide employment in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The project is in the hands of P.F.R.A. The department merely allocates certain funds from this vote to permit P.F.R.A. to go ahead with the survey. When the time comes to proceed with the project, appropriations will be made from the P.F.R.A. vote in the usual way. Only the Minister of Agriculture can give the information asked for.

The Minister of Agriculture within the last few days did give some information in regard to the South Saskatchewan river project; he said that $110,000 had been spent during the year on survey proceedings. The total amount of

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
expenditure for the coming year,, according to the estimates, is to be $1,000,000. I should like to find out what projects particularly are in the mind of the government, how that expenditure of $1,000,000 is to be made, and how it is to be distributed.
The South Saskatchewan river project, according to the present views of the Minister of Agriculture, cannot be proceeded with for a period of two years. I think it should be proceeded with now. Extensive exploratory and engineering work has been done, but the government's attitude is that the work shall not go ahead. Is the minister able to say how much of the $1,000,000 will be expended, or is to be expended, this year?
I wish to bring to the minister's attention another project in Saskatchewan which, if properly developed and encouraged, would attract to that province many tourists who today are not coming in. I refer to Watrous lake, some ninety miles east of Saskatoon, a lake which for over two hundred years has been recognized by the Indians living on the plains as possessing peculiar medicinal qualities. In the last few years that lake has gone back because of drought and because the springs that ordinarily feed it have been covered over by an incrustation of chemicals resulting from heat and evaporation. Is that the type of project which the department of reconstruction would consider a proper one on which to expend moneys under this item? I am not asking for the expenditure of money on anything but self-liquidating projects, and I suggest to the minister that this is one that would pay large dividends in increased tourist traffic and in the numbers who would come from various parts of the United States for treatment in this lake.
About three years ago the minister stated that his department had plans ready for public projects and was prepared to go ahead on short notice. He said that particular attention would be given by his department to projects designed to develop basic industries and to press forward vigorously, improvement in transportation and the opening of northern regions. I would ask him what is being done to carry out the views he then expressed.
Today our only hope for the development of the north country is through the instrumentality of private enterprise. In Saskatchewan-and I am not entering into any controversy on the subject-no government can afford to invest risk capital in exploratory work for the development of our natural resources. In fact, as far as gas and oil development is concerned, that has been turned over by the government of Saskatchewan to private interests. We all realize that

governments, however great the potentialities in natural resources, cannot afford to risk the taxpayers' money on projects without knowing for certain that they will actually return dividends.
There is great risk in the development of these resources. Recently I noticed that the total amount of return to private companies in Alberta since the development of the oil resources in that province has been $55,000,000, while the total amount expended in risk capital since oil was first discovered there has been $65,000,000.
I should like to know what the government intends to do during the coming year to open up communications with the north country, so that opportunities will be available to private enterprise to go in and develop. We need in Saskatchewan, as in the other western provinces, the opening of roads and the development of power, which after all, in the northland, must be a matter of government expenditure-as in the Yellowknife district by virtue of legislation introduced the other day and now, I believe, passed by parliament.
What plans has the minister to encourage the development of the eighty-five per cent of our country which is largely undeveloped today? I do not think that any government can enter into that development but I believe that one of the responsibilities of the minister, as head of this department, is the surveying of the country. Indeed, he himself said three years ago that these were his plans, and then, a general survey having been made, funds would be advanced on behalf of the state to the end that opportunities would be made available to private companies prepared to risk their capital in the uncertain development of our resources.
My questions therefore are these: (1) How much will be expended this 3rear on the South Saskatchewan development? (2) Does a project such as I have mentioned, the one at Watrous lake, come within the purview of this estimate? (3) Will the minister give the country the benefit of his experience in the matter of the, expansion and encouragement of development of our natural resources, to the end that in our north country we shall give to private enterprise the opportunity which too often is denied it because of the costly expenditures private enterprise would have to undertake to make these resources accessible?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
This $1,000,000 refers to no known project at the moment. If the project were known, it would not be included in this vote but would be in a special item. This vote is to meet unforeseen conditions. The vote

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
was originally 85,000,000 and was reduced to $1,000,000, because we have learned over the years that in times like these there are not many unforeseen situations that have to be met apart from those provided for through the normal estimates. The drawings on the fund have been small. We have started projects where some unusual situation made it imperative that no time be lost.

How much was
drawn out of the fund last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I gave the figure.
Yes, but I am asking for it again.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: $591,000. Watrous lake is wholly in the province of Saskatchewan. Any development of the type indicated must be sponsored by the province. The same remarks as I made regarding the Red Deer apply to a dam on the South Saskatchewan river. It is a project which is being carried out by the P.F.R.A. Certain expenditures were made for borings last year, and money was appropriated from this account. But this year and in the future, appropriations will be in the estimates of the P.F.R.A.
No part of the million dollars will be used on the South Saskatchewan project?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Not unless an emergency arises which indicates that it should be so used.

What does the
minister mean by an emergency?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Some necessary and unforeseen expenditure that the government believes is sufficiently urgent to warrant an appropriation from this vote. The South Saskatchewan is one of the most difficult engineering problems that has ever been tackled in this country. Part of the problem is to build a high earth dam on material that has no known bottom. In building grain elevators in that country we used to drive all the piles we could get, of as great a length as we could get, build on it, load the elevator, say a prayer and watch it settle a few inches. You cannot do that with a dam. You must find something to put a da.m on in order to make .the project feasible. That is involved in the present exploration. It is no easy problem. However, it is being tackled by the best engineering skill that can be made available.
Do any of the engineers in the minister's department make reports on this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.

Or make any
investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
No. We do on occasion, but not on this particular project. It is too big a project for casual engineering. It requires a special Staff.
I think that answers the question. Was there another one?
What about the northern area? What is being done there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Where the province has shown an interest in an area, we sometimes render assistance in opening it up. A case in point is the road from Alberta into the Yellowknife region. The road has been built, or is under construction, connecting Alberta with the Northwest Territories. That road within the Northwest Territories is being paid for by the federal government, and some assistance has been given to the Alberta section of the road. The federal government is just, completing a power plant in the Yellowknife area. A bill has been before the house at this session to set up a power commission. Ordinarily it is the job of each separate province to develop power within its boundaries. That is a job the provinces are glad to undertake because it is usually a profitable operation. But in the Northwest Territories the federal government is the government, and it is carrying out there the duties that would ordinarily be carried out by a province if that area were included in a province.
With regard to northern Manitoba, some important discoveries were made in the vicinity of Flin Flon. There again the government is giving some assistance to the province in building a road to open up the area. Certain assistance has been given to British Columbia in opening up certain areas.
Which ones?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I cannot say offhand. It would not come from this estimate or this vote. The votes were made in the usual way. I cannot say which ones. The Department of Mines and Resources will be able to tell my hon. friend that.

Construction is made more difficult because of the difficulty in getting cement. Some builders have told me that last year the Canada Cement Company closed a manufacturing plant in Ontario, and that at least one million bags of cement would have to be provided from the province of Quebec in order to fill the gap. I wonder if that is true. I would ask the minister, who must know about the matter, for some information with regard to the closing of the

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
Ontario plant of the Canada Cement Company and the possibility of securing cement by those who intend to build houses. At the present time it is most difficult for those who are building to put in the foundations of any building they are constructing. I would be grateful to the minister if he would give us some explanation about the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The position of cement is vastly better this year than it was last. The addition to the plant of the Canada Cement Company in Montreal has been completed and is in full operation. The addition to the cement plant at Belleville is in full operation. The addition to the Exshaw plant is in full operation, I believe; in fact, I am sure it is by now. I think the capacity has been expanded-I hesitate to give the amount- by something of the order of a million barrels a year as compared with last year.
Was one Ontario plant closed last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Only for repairs or expansion. All the cement capacity of the country is operating, and I am told by the industry that it is expected that there will be plenty of cement this year.
There is a plant at Lake-field which has been closed for some years. Is it to be reopened?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If the plant has been closed for some years, the chances are that it could not be reopened.

Last night the minister
stated that the department of reconstruction would be wound up within six or seven months. As I understand it, one of the principal functions of the department has been to take a look at the country as a whole, from a broad view, and to decide where projects will be undertaken. I think that was a useful job. But what is to happen when the department folds up? Is some other department of the government to take on the function of viewing the picture across the country as a whole and deciding where this help should be given? That of course is important, not only from the point of view of furnishing employment in bad times, but also for the long range development of the country. I think it is important that we should know just which department of the government is to cariy on this useful work once the department of reconstruction folds up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The department of reconstruction was formed for the purpose of looking after the transition from war to peace. We feel that that work has been accomplished.

However, there are certain continuing functions which we believe should be merged into the permanent plan of operation. Two branches were concerned with the work suggested by my hon. friend. One was the economic research branch, which studies the figures collected by the bureau of statistics, and also collects figures independently and prepares reports from time to time on the state of the country, calling attention to any situation that requires special attention. The other was the public projects branch whose duty it was to encourage self-liquidating or necessary public projects, and to have them available whenever the manpower and materials situation make it possible to carry out such projects. That will be a continuing branch, and both those branches will be merged1 in the Department of Trade and Commerce.
This will not be under the Department of Public Works or the Department of Mines and Resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The plan at the present time is that it wall be under the Department of Trade and Commerce. There may be some re-adjustment later. At the moment, consolidation is going on between the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Reconstruction and Supply.

Has the minister's department done any survey work across Manitoba in connection with a new trans-Canada highway? I know certain work was done, but I believe it was done by the provincial authorities in connection with the re-routing of the highway. Actually I should think the trans-Canada highway would be in the mind of the minister, because it is related to the employment part of his program. If no survey has been made, is it in contemplation; and is it the ultimate intention of the department to build the trans-Canada highway across Manitoba and western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The policy has always been that the route of the trans-Canada highway is a matter for each province to recommend and the federal government to approve. Highways are the responsibility of the provinces. The federal government has neither the authority nor the machinery to build highways in the provinces. Any surveys having to-do with the trans-Canada highway in Manitoba would be made by that province.

In connection with the closing out of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, what would happen to housing projects? Also, will the minister make-a statement about the rumour that any com-

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
munity wishing to begin a wartime housing project must make application before a certain time?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: All the housing functions of the government have been concentrated in the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a crown company. It has been customary every year to draw a deadline at a certain date as the cut-off for the program of that year. Obviously a house started in September, 1948, cannot be considered as part of the 1948 program, because it will not be completed in that year. The government does not desire to begin the building of houses in the autumn so that they will have to be completed in the winter. The process is too expensive. The program for 1948 was cut off, I believe, on June 1. This autumn we shall probably be considering the program for 1949.
But it is the intention of the government to carry on the housing program under another department in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will continue to be that body. At the present time it reports to the Minister of Renconstruction and Supply. In future it will report either to him or to some other minister, and its functions will be carried on.

The minister has intimated that the provinces are responsible for the designation of the route. Is there any set contribution that the dominion government makes towards that project, or is it a matter of negotiation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is no policy which provides for contributions from the federal government toward the building of any highway at the present time-except by special arrangement ; and that is usually confined to the opening up of new areas.
That is, there never has been any such-*

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Oh, there has been a policy, yes-other days, other policies. There was a policy in the thirties, when employment was a key consideration, at which time the cost was divided fifty-fifty. At the present time, however, it is impossible to tackle a big project on account of lack of manpower. When it becomes possible to consider such a project, a new policy will be established.
Is there among the future unemployment relief projects or programs of the government any blueprint for the trans-Canada highway?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
If we see any sign of widespread unemployment we will proceed to make
a blueprint. But at the present time we have not a blueprint and we do not think one is necessary.

Or over the strait of Canso.

speechtext: Now-

T. he DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Just a minute. If the committee consents that anything and everything can be discussed under this item, the Chair will agree. I have simply drawn attention to the fact that the item does not cover these things.

On the point of order, if the chairman says that this item does not cover such projects as the trans-Canada highway, then I think it is up to the chairman to say what subjects can be discussed under this item. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Costing not more than

I agree with the minister that he should not set an amount now, because he has stated that the government would consider this at the appropriate time. I submit that the trans-Canada highway can be discussed under this item, and I think, Mr. Chairman, you should rule accordingly.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I suggest to hon. members that they should not spend time talking about the chairman's ruling. Apparently it is the wish of the committee that the discussion be wide open.
It will not take long.

The minister's statement indicates that the government has no intention of proceeding with the trans-Canada highway project until there is a period of unemployment, and that the government also believes that the initiative must come from the provinces. I am afraid that that is not a proper policy. Certainly it is not in line with the wishes of western Canada. We believe that there should be a paved highway from coast to coast, and that it will never be built until the dominion government takes the lead.
At present if anyone from British Columbia wants to drive to the east, or if anyone from British Columbia happens to be in the east- for example, a member of parliament-and wants to drive back to British Columbia with a new car, he does not think for one minute of going through Canada. He gets into the United States by the shortest route, travels across the United States as far as he possibly can, and then comes back into Canada.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
And spends United States dollars in the process.

If he can get them. That has been the position for a long time, and it creates a serious situation. It makes it that much more difficult to build up a strong nation. I think one of the most important policies that could be adopted by any Canadian government would, be the completion of a paved highway from coast to coast.
A person in British Columbia never thinks of driving to Alberta; it just never enters his head. If he goes for a drive he goes to Washington or Oregon or California; he would not think of driving across to Calgary. The same thing applies to most of the people on the prairies. They seldom think of driving through the mountains to British Columbia, because the road is poor. It is a ridiculous situation to have in a nation which we hope will be one of the leading nations of the world. It is not good enough to put off the construction of the trans-Canada highway until-
Who builds the roads over in the United States?

We tried to get you a bridge a few minutes ago. It is not good enough to put off building a first-class trans-Canada highway until there is a period of unemployment or until we can get the nine provinces to take a lead. The lead in this connection must come from the dominion. I am sorry to learn this morning that the policy of the government is as it has been enunciated by the minister.

I have received from
British Columbia many letters and resolutions indicating a great interest in this matter. I do not concede that the dominion government cannot have any interest or responsibility in connection with a trans-Canada highway. A trans-Canada highway, because of changed transportation conditions, is as much a necessity today as were the railroads before and after confederation.
I do not believe the trans-Canada highway can be built by the provinces. Some of the provincial roads already in existence could be used as part of the trans-Canada highway, but I am satisfied that sooner or later the federal government will have to give some assistance. If it has to give assistance, then I think it should have some say in deciding what the route should be. I do not agree that the federal government should provide funds for projects and then have no control over them.
With the relatively high employment existing at the present time perhaps this would not be a good time for the provinces or the federal government or both to start actual construction on a project of this kind. But a policy should be announced and the necessary surveys made so that when labour and materials are easier than they are now, the provinces and the federal government will be able to go ahead with the project in a properly planned way.
I am not sure whether the minister and the government have such a policy in mind, but ultimately they will have to have one, because the people of Canada will demand it; and they are demanding it now.

For three years I have been trying to bring this matter separately before the house under a resolution which would deal with this matter alone, but that has not been feasible. I support what has been said here this morning, except that I do not agree with the member for Vancouver East that the time is not ripe to make a start on this construction. Our provinces are building roads now which might form part of a trans-Canada highway system, and they should have now the financial assistance that will eventually be given to them under a trans-Canada highway policy.
I agree that the federal government should not be expected merely to contribute funds, but should have a say in the standards of construction and maintenance, and in the location of the highway. The most logical way to proceed would be along the lines followed in the United States, where a federal highways commission is set up, which, in conjunction with the states, works out the location of the roads and the standards of construction and maintenance. When the states have built the roads in accordance with the agreed specifications, the federal contribution is payable. That would be the logical way to do it in Canada. In the United States if the road is maintained in accordance with the agreed specifications, a yearly contribution is made towards the maintenance of that highway system. The policing of the road, traffic laws, and so forth, are in provincial hands. But the federal government, through the highways commission on which the states have representation, lays down the standards of construction and of maintenance. The federal government's contribution is fifty per cent. I think we should follow that precedent here and make a start now, so that the provinces which have to build and maintain their roads would be entitled to federal assistance in respect of the roads which fall within the trans-Canada highway system.
The commission might well take into consideration also the question whether we should have only one, or two or more trans-Canada roads, and should be making its plans for the location of these roads to encourage the provinces in the road building they are now doing

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
which will become part of the highway system. The provinces should receive assistance in that work now. Then the provinces, particularly the western provinces, could devote their own resources to their own main problems, which include the building of roads in the new areas to be developed; and the federal funds would help to take care of the main road question.
While I agree with all the principles put forward this morning, I do not agree with the member for Vancouver East that no start can be made on actual construction now. I feel that we could make a start along the lines I have suggested, without making extra demands on labour and building materials.

I am not objecting to what the British Columbia members do, who are well represented on both sides of the house. But houses are needed ahead of highways. I point out to the minister that an agreement was made by the city of Toronto with this government and the provincial government under which the federal government was to pay one-third of the cost of some housing projects, and I hope that commitment will be lived up to.

I do not propose to discuss the trans-Canada highway, except to point out that last year thirteen of us, including members from various parties, supported a program in favour of the southern route for a trans-Canada highway. Therefore I am thoroughly in favour of what has been said this morning in support of a trans-Canada highway.
I wish to say a few words on the Red Deer diversion scheme. There are several aspects of this scheme which are worthy of consideration by the minister of reconstruction. In the first place, the Red Deer diversion scheme is designed to put water on pasture land in what is known as short-grass country. The short-grass country extends in various directions from Medicine Hat, and the same kind of country is to be found in the area to be served by the Red Deer diversion scheme.
Those who are not familiar with western terminology may not know the significance of short grass. Short grass is exceedingly nutritive. Cattle will finish more rapidly on short grass than on any other kind of natural forage that I know. We can therefore see that this area is exceedingly valuable as a source of feed. The soil is very rich. The grass grows rapidly and abundantly as long as there is water on the land. The soil is not inclined to alkalization. We do not have to worry about spoiling that land with too much water because the land is well drained.

May I say for the benefit of those who are interested in irrigation projects in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, that there is danger in irrigation schemes of spoiling the land through alkalization if it is not well drained or susceptible of being well drained. The land I speak of is well drained and is not subject to alkalization.
There are 500.000 acres of land involved in the Red Deer diversion scheme, using water only out of the Red Deer. If you add water from the North Saskatchewan, 900,000 acres could be brought under water, all exceedingly productive.
The land is gently rolling, the slopes not precipitous; the water will not run off-a very important factor in any irrigation scheme.
There is one reason why I am particularly interested in the Red Deer diversion. I may seem to be looking too far into the future, but I do not think I am. The Red Deer diversion is naturally a complementary scheme to such a project as the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project which the minister has done so much to help forward, a scheme designed primarily to put water on agricultural land on which it is proposed to raise sugar beets, canning crops and other cultivated crops. The Red Deer diversion scheme is not so valuable for cultivated crops as it is to provide forage for stock. There are, in the area adjacent to the Red Deer diversion scheme, great stretches of land which, being in the Palliser Triangle, do not receive sufficient precipitation to enable the land to support regular settlement. It does receive just enough water to make it pretty good pasture for cattle, so that probably four acres would supply the needs of one animal. A person could not make a living on a small amount of that land. But if it is not used in production of stock it remains idle and of no value to the Canadian economy.
The minister can readily see that such an area could well be used in the Canadian economy for the production of beef which would be fattened down in the areas where the sugar beet factories are. It is thus extremely important, especially if we go forward with an extensive development of the beet sugar industry, as we should, in the area which the minister is now proposing to irrigate under the Lethbridge southeast conservation project, involving, as the minister knows, about 350,000 acres of land.
Considering the fact that we are going forward with the St. Mary river project, the Red Deer diversion scheme ought to be developed as a complementary project.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
May I give a few other facts about this project?-and then I shall resume my seat. I am informed that the main dam for the Red Deer diversion project will back up water to a depth of 150 feet on the Red Deer river, which means a great deal of water. From the reservoir produced by the dam it is proposed to carry the water by canal to lake Hamilton. It is thought that the cost of building the dam and carrying the water to lake Hamilton would amount to around $7,000,000, which in days like these is not a great deal of money, especially bearing in mind the tremendous value to the Canadian economy which could result from the expenditure of this money.
There is another important aspect of this particular project. At the present time, as the minister knows, all over the west there is a great deal of run-off. Where the land is covered with short grass, nearly all the water that- Mis in anything like a rapid rain, or in a snowstorm, which melts quickly, runs off and we get no good from it ait all. In this particular area there is -a broad basin from which a vast amount of water yearly runs off. That water could be arrested without too much expenditure in the Red Deer diversion scheme by constructing appropriate dams here and there at the mouth of lake Hamilton and various other small lakes. Thus a great deal of good could be derived by saving that amount of water which now runs away into the Hudson bay to waste.
There is another lake beside lake Hamilton which is also important to this scheme, namely, Buffalo lake. When I tell hon. members that Buffalo lake is fourteen miles long and eight miles wide, they will realize that we are not talking in terms of small matters when we discuss the Red Deer diversion scheme. The cost of the whole project is estimated at about $15,000,000. That is about the amount which is to be spent on the St. Mary river project.
There is one more aspect of the matter. We have had bitter experiences this year in the floods on the Fraser river. In any area in which there occurs occasionally abnormal precipitation, either of snow or of rain, we are apt to have serious floods. We might have serious floods on the prairie rivers. I have seen very serious floods at Lethbridge, Medicine Hat. and Cardston. We did not happen to have them this year, but we could have had them. The Red Deer river is capable of giving us a serious flood problem. The town of Drumheller suffered this year. The construction of this project would help to overcome the danger of floods on the Red Deer river, because it is proposed to draw the water
from the main reservoir into lake Hamilton, and this, as the minister can see, would auitomatioallly distribute the water over a wide area. From the canal which draws the water from the main reservoir into lake Hamilton it is proposed to cut a canal of about a mile into Buffalo lake. There another tremendous amount of water can be stored, which could be used either to replenish the water of the Red Deer in case of low water, or to supply water to lake Hamilton and the land under the project.
The minister can see from what I have given in this rough outline that the project is really in a class by itself and worthy of special consideration.
May I deal with one or two other matters? It is the responsibility of Canada at the present time to supply food. Nearly everybody is worrying about food. The world is actually short of food. I wish to refer to an article which I shall not go into in any detail. It is headed "Want still threatens the world." It appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 22, 1948. The subtitle reads as follows: "Sir John Boyd Orr reiterates his grim warning that the nations should be growing food instead of making preparations for war." In the article appeared these words:
But as he showed' in notable reports, most of the people of Britain were not adequately nourished and half the world's population normally suffers disease, disability, and premature death because of not having enough food. Now the world's high birthrate is intensifying the problem.
As the minister very well knows, when people get hungry they are capable of doing a good many extreme things, including going to war. Nations which are abundantly blessed by Providence, such as the United States and Canada, simply must be prepared to assume a greater and greater responsibility in the world's program of producing food for a hungry people. We cannot afford to defer this matter long; the people are hungry now, and they have been ever since the war. The population is rapidly increasing. This is important in connection with this project because of the fact, as I have indicated, that by developing this project we can produce great quantities of beef which can be finished in the sugar beet areas, greatly to the advantage of the whole country. The Red Deer diversion scheme is not necessarily a reconstruction project or part of a reconstruction program for Canada; it is rather a part of the reconstruction scheme for the world. This gives the matter considerable importance.
I trust that hon. members of the committee will pardon me for having detained them

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
as long as I have, but I did think that this matter was worthy of special attention, at this time.
I see bright prospects for the completion of the trans-Canada highway.
You have good eyesight.
Where do you see it?

During the provincial election the Premier of Ontario, along with his supporters, promised that the Ontario part of the road would be completed. Of course there are a good many people who think that the premier of the province keeps his promises. I think he will keep this promise if he considers it of practical use. Since he has visited the head of the lakes and knows what we have there as an attraction for tourists from the east and from the west, we are sure that he will do his part.
In the past the Minister of Trade and Commerce has shown a willingness to co-operate with anybody and everybody for the good of Canada. When we think of what we have at the bead of the lakes to sell to the rest of Canada, we believe that the province will do its part, and I am sure the dominion will do its part.

It is evident that there is a national need and a national demand for a highway system across Canada. The organization of highway associations, resolutions from boards of trade, and meeting of the highway ministers from various provinces have revealed that there is not only a need but a willingness on the part of the provinces to co-operate with the dominion in any such scheme. The debates in this bouse reveal that there is a demand from the Canadian people for a highway system which would be worthy of this country.
It is evident also that the nine provinces cannot build this road by themselves. Some of the provinces have extensive highway programs, which take in practically everything they can possibly do. By means of co-operation between the federal government and the provincial authorities, along lines similar to those followed in the United States, I think it is possible for the dominion to inaugurate a system, and I am surprised that steps have not been taken towards laying the foundation for negotiation between the provinces and the federal government with respect to this important project.
It is evident that in the prairies not only the provincial governments but the people themselves are willing to assist. It is fully realized that the people do not want construction materials to be used in the building of high-

ways if they are necessary for housing, for houses at the present time are more important than highways. At the same time there are vast stretches in the prairies over which highway construction would not be very expensive. They have the tar sands, and they could proceed with highway construction that would be both cheap and easily done, compared with British Columbia. But British Columbia has shown its willingness to act.
I should like to know whether or not any steps have been taken towards negotiation between the federal government and the provincial authorities in order to lay plans for proper co-operation so that this important national project may be undertaken. Has there been any negotiation at all, or any approach from the provinces in the matter?

Mr. Chairman, I have been
waiting for the past twenty minutes to get the floor in order to add my little piece on the question of a trang-Canada highway, but I have been unable to get the eye of the chairman because I am so far away from him.
I should like to comment briefly on the reply given to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie by the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. The minister stated that it was the responsibility of the different provinces to plan and construct a trans-Canada highway. In my opinion the federal government should take the initiative. We shall have no continuous highway if we leave it to the individual provinces, for the reason that there are a number of people who feel that the routes which they advocate should be constructed.
In my opinion the government should adopt the suggestion made by an organization set up recently at Saskatoon'-last November 29, I believe-which recommended a trans-Canada highway commission to co-ordinate the efforts of the different provinces in cooperation with the dominion, 'because that would be the proper solution of the project.
The Yellowhead route for the trans-Canada highway has been advocated by many people in the prairie provinces. At my home town of Vermilion, on October 15 last, a meeting was held, attended by 127 delegates representing the district between Edmonton and North Battleford inclusive, and I understand that a report of that meeting has been forwarded to the dominion government, as have been briefs on former occasions dealing with the trans-Canada highway Yellowhead route. In these briefs it was pointed out that the Yellowhead route is shorter, and presents fewer engineering difficulties than

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
the others that have been proposed. There is much less snow on it in the winter, and therefore it is passable for more months of the year than the other suggested routes. I understand that route was picked out by the engineers of the Canadian Pacific Railway many years ago, but for some reason it was later abandoned.
A survey by engineers would show, I believe, that the proper route to take would be from Winnipeg to Saskatoon, Lloydminster, Vermilion, Vegreville and Edmonton, then on to Vancouver, with another branch to be built to Prince Rupert.
I have said on this vote part of what I intended to say on the estimates of the Department of Public Works, in case I am not here when they come up. I see the Minister of Public Works in his seat, and I hope he will take note of my remarks. Many things can be said in favour of the Yellowhead route, and I believe the time has long gone by when it should have been built.
Like many other members from the west, I have motored across Canada at different times, but I have not taken a chance on motoring all the way through the dominion. I have followed routes to the south where there are good roads. I think it is a disgrace to this dominion that there is not an allweather highway from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I have been trying to get in my main question on this subject of a trans-Canada highway, and I should like to make a suggestion to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: This has nothing to do with the trans-Canada highway, I know nothing about the trans-Canada highway; I will not answer questions about it, and after that you can go on with your questions.

I will not make a speech, but, I wish to offer a suggestion. I suggest that the minister confer with the Minister of Mines and Resources, the Minister of Public Works, and the Minister of National Defence, and perhaps also, as has been suggested, have someone originate discussions with the provinces, with a view at least to having someone take the lead in this matter and co-ordinate the whole thing so as to have a plan prepared. From the standpoint of bringing in tourists it is important to the Department of Mines and Resources. Public works might also be involved, and certainly national defence. The provinces are interested, and I do not think there is one of them which would present any obstacle to the federal government stepping in
and taking the initiative in the construction of a trans-Canada highway. I think the minister of the department whose estimates we are now considering is the one who can best take the lead in originating discussions among the various departments concerned, and in giving consideration to this project, the necessity for which has been emphasized so much this morning by various members.

When the hon. member for Cape Breton South was speaking on item 409 he stressed once again the strait of Canso connection-that is, between Cape Breton Island and the mainland of Nova Scotia. I do not wish to deal with this matter any more than to say that I concur in what the hon. member has said; and whether it should be a causeway, bridge or tunnel, I would be prepared to leave to the best judgment of capable engineers. I wish to say that this is not a community matter, nor is it a maritime matter. It is a national necessity for the business that is being done in that part of Nova Scotia. Therefore as a maritimer I am glad to support what the hon. member for Cape Breton South has already said.
I was surprised to learn from the minister of reconstruction that this department is now what might be termed a passing show. A few years ago when this department was organized it was heralded across Canada with trumpets sounding as one of the greatest departments of government for the benefit of Canada and all the provinces that was ever inaugurated at Ottawa. At the same time this department advises the provinces to set up similar offices or organizations by means of which to get in contact with the federal government and bring before them what the provinces desire with regard to the different projects they have in mind in their own interests.
What has this reconstruction department done? We find-and I intend to speak of our own province in particular-that the work of this department has been practically nil. However, it has been of some service to the government. It was an excellent vote-catcher in 1945, and again in 1947, in the provincial election. The projects that have been outlined in my province to the'federal department were projects such as the West Point-Buctouche ferry system, a super-highway from Borden to Charlottetown, and the construction of the ^ Brighton bridge, by means of which, in conjunction with the super-highway from Borden, the distance from Borden to Charlottetown would be shortened by some twenty miles. Both major political parties made definite commitments with reference to those projects that were placed before the
[The Chairman.]
federal government. As I said, they were given prior to an election, but the people had some faith, and believed that the government, if elected, would fulfil those promises. So far, however, we have nothing but the bare promises.
In this connection I might say that we have been advised today by the minister, and also by the chairman on several occasions, that we should not have anything to say about these projects at the present time, that we must simply forget them. In other words, they have told us that we are not supposed to speak about road building as one of the projects. In the course of the discussion I learned from various people who were discussing this matter-

With all due respect, Mr. Chairman-

I shall now mention a matter which was much in the limelight prior to the last two elections-the West Point-Buctouche ferry proposal. The people in Prince Edward Island were not asking for too much. They have already secured at Buctouche a guarantee for a landing pier at no cost whatsoever to the federal government. They have also secured, through the Saint John Dry Dock concern, the use of two suitable boats for this ferry route again at no cost to the federal department. All the people are asking with reference to this project is that a pier be built at West Point for the benefit of the farmers in that community. Besides, of course, they will be looking for a subsidy in connection with the service that is to be rendered. If under these circumstances that project is not to be definitely taken up at this session or during this fall, I believe the people should be definitely so advised so that they may take upon themselves the responsibility of making other

arrangements for transporting their crops instead of having the long haul to which they are now subjected.
I wish also to mention in passing that we were definitely promised, under this reconstruction policy and reconstruction department, that consideration would be given to harbour improvements in the city of Charlottetown. Consideration was to be given to the building of a marine railway slip. I mention these things so that we may not be brushed off too easily with regard to the promises that have been made. We were hoping that after 1935 the work would be completed, but nothing has been done, with the exception of the repeated promise that this super-highway would be built.
Another highway was built by the federal government from Hunter river to Rustico. This highway was built entirely by the federal government, without one cent of cost to the provincial government. These projects have been started, and the federal government should take upon itself the fulfilment of what the Department of Reconstruction and Supply has led people to believe would be implemented.
I hope the minister will give us some assurance that the projects which have been mentioned1 will have some chance of completion witihin the next six months.

In what I shall say I am not holding the minister responsible, because he will remember that some few months ago when he took over this branch I told him he rvas asking for trouble. I am interested in some twenty projects in the Hamilton area. basis. I learn that in every case it was let on a cost-plus basis, and in some cases the cost of conversion was almost double that of the understanding between the owmers and the department.
