its. Wartime Housing Limited, $50,000,000.

When, as the minister indicated, this department closes up in six or seven months, who will be responsible for the supervision of wartime housing projects and other housing projeots under construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The present minister is the one designated to be in charge of wartime housing. Until some change is .made, the present arrangement will continue.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a question having to do with the request made by certain municipalities in British Columbia for increased returns from the lots now occupied by wartime houses. I know this is the case with Kamloops and I am informed the same

condition applies to other municipalities. The municipality finds that it can no longer service these lots at the figure agreed upon with the government when the houses were first built, which was from $24 to $30 per lot per year. I understand that the government has entered into an arrangement whereby the city will receive in the neighbourhood of $80 per year, but the tenants now find that there will be an increase in their rental.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.
How is it to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The rent is just the same.
I have received a petition from practically every tenant of the wartime houses built in Kamloops protesting against being charged increased rentals.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The rental is just the same. The city of Kamloops in its judgment has made a certain assessment against the tenants for taxes, and the government has agreed to collect the additional amount and remit it to the city.
Although it is not rent that the government is collecting, it is-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It will be collected by the government and paid over to the city which made the assessment.

These projects were intended to provide low-rental houses, and as far as I can make out from the correspondence I have had with the department, so far it is not denied that the city requires a greater amount in respect to these lots than it is now getting. If they continue at the present rate they will have to impose an unfair tax burden on the ordinary property holder in the city.
An agreement, which the minister has just mentioned, has been arrived at between the city and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. If that agreement is carried out, it means that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, which is in effect the federal government, will not bear any portion of the increased administration costs with which the city is faced. The result is that these houses are no longer the low-rental houses they were originally intended to be.
Although it is not rent that the government is charging, to the tenant it amounts to an increased rental. If it is the purpose of these projects to provide low-rental housing to those in the low income brackets, particularly returned veterans, I think it would be proper for the federal government to pay a portion of the increased costs of the municipality. The government should assume at least half' and let the tenant pay the other half.

__________Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
As I say, I am in correspondence with the department about the matter, and I have not as yet received a definite reply. They suggest that they do not understand the purport of my representations. I hope they understand it now. I think the federal government should pay at least half of the increased costs, with the tenant making up the other half.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The position of the crown is quite clear. The houses were built under a tax agreement with the city. The rentals provide for a reasonable return on the capital investment and also for agreed taxes. The city agreed that the charge per house would be $25 a year, or thereabouts. However, the city has since changed its mind about the taxes that it requires from these houses. The crown has not changed its position one iota. It requires so much as a return on the investment ; an amount which has not changed. The federal government has not imposed any greater burden on anyone. The city has increased its requirements from $24 to $70 or $80. As a convenience the crown agreed to collect that for the city, although it is under no obligation to do so. It could easily have said, "Make your own collections," but it did not. It is co-operating with the city to the extent that it is collecting the city's levy along with its own rentals. The rentals have not changed.

In other words, the crown will not assist the city by assuming some portion of the increased burden? Is it not admitted that the city erred on the side of generosity when it fixed its charges at from $24 to $30 per lot per year? Surely it cannot be denied that that is too little to charge for servicing a lot?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: All I can say is that the amount was agreed upon with the city. They signed an agreement voluntarily, and we assumed that there were intelligent people in Kamloops. We have to assume that. If my hon. friend owns a house and the city requires more taxes, I am sure he will pay them.

But the city entered into that agreement only because it was under compulsion to do so. It is not quite correct for the minister to say that they were not under any compulsion. They were under compulsion because they regarded it as their moral duty to try to supply low-rental accommodation for their citizens. All costs have gone up since then. The return to the city was low enough at that time, but the city was willing to accept it because of the compulsion I have spoken of. Costs having gone up, the federal government should assume at
least a portion of them. The city would still be getting less than it receives from private taxpayers, and therefore the other taxpayers would still be helping to provide this low rental accommodation. My suggestion is that the whole burden should not be placed on the city.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am not placing any burden on the city; the city is placing a burden on the tenants.

Do not permit the city to assume the whole burden of increased costs; the federal government should help.
Mr. HOI\E: The city is not assuming any burden.

The minister has said that the crown requires a certain return as interest on its investment. The investment of the crown is to be returned by the payments made each month. Why should not the city get back its investment? Why should the city assume the burden of servicing these properties at less than cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We do not ask them to.

No, but you say that if they do not do that, they have to pass on the whole cost to the taxpayers. In other words it is no longer a low-rental housing project. The whole investment is to be returned with interest, and the tenants will have to pay full taxes or the city will have to service these properties at a loss. These projects are certainly not fulfilling the purpose which the city understood they would when it entered into the agreement, that of providing low rental housing with an element of subsidization.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The city knew exactly what the houses would be like; they knew that they involved a rental of some $19 or $20 a month to the government, plus taxes of about $24 per year to the city. That was well known to all. The government has not changed its position. Its amortization and interest charges are exactly what they were then. My hon. friend is trying to say that the government has changed something, but the government has changed nothing at all. Will he explain wherein the government has done any great injustice to the city?
I will try to do it again. All costs have gone up. That is not the fault of the city, nor is it the fault of the taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Nor of the government.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

I will not enter into a debate as to whether it is the fault of the government, but these costs have gone up, and what I am asking the government to do is to change their present position. Let them enter into a further arrangement with the city to share the burden of the increased cost, fifty per cent each, and do not ask the property owners, the taxpayers, to pay any share of that increased cost. This will be doing what we have in effect frequently urged the government to do-provide low-rental housing with an element of subsidization.
I would like someone to take care of me in regard to my property.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: This discussion is getting back to subsidized housing. The position is this. The city is not sacrificing anything. It is getting taxes from these houses just as from any privately owned houses. That is the business of the city. We cannot interfere between the city and the taxpayers, and we are not inclined to; we are co-operative.
The city would be glad if you were to share the increased cost.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I know that. My hon. friend may think that is the logical thing to do with the public purse, but I differ. The increase in the old rental is trivial in comparison with the increased costs. It is still the lowest rental housing in Kamloops or anywhere else.

Will the minister explain why the government undertook to collect these taxes for the city? Apparently the position in Vancouver is that originally an agreement was made between the city and the corporation and the houses were rented at an agreed figure. Then the city threatened to levy a tax on the tenants as distinct from a tax on the land. The government negotiated a contract with the city, without consulting the tenants at all, and apparently agreed to collect the assessment that had been levied on the tenants.
The next thing that happened, according to a brief I have here from the Wartime Housing Tenants Association of Vancouver, dated early in May or about the end of April, a copy of which has been submitted to the minister, was that Central Mortgage and Housing then sent to these tenants what it is referred to in the brief as "a notice to quit," but it seems to me a notice of increased rental. It reads:
Under the terms of a resolution passed by the city of Vancouver, dated February 24, 1948, this corporation (Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation) has been requested to provide increased payments in lieu of taxes to the city of Vancouver. In order to provide these re-

quested increased payments in lieu of taxes, your rent will have to be increased by a similar amount.
That was the notice sent by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to these tenants, who apparently knew nothing about the deal made between the city and Central Mortgage and Housing for an increased rental. Apparently it was done in the face of an understanding between the city and the tenants association that no change would be made without the tenants being permitted to make representations. I admit that the government is not responsible for any agreement of the kind made by the city, but the agreement makes it just that much more unfair from the point of view of the tenants. I should like to know why the government agreed with the city to collect these taxes, which were being levied, not on the government but on the tenants, without the tenants being given an opportunity to make representations.
A further question is this. This brief says that throughout there has been a suggestion that the tenants would be able to purchase the houses, but no sale terms have ever been announced. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has not yet told the tenants on what terms they may buy these properties. Many of the tenants might like to purchase the properties; if they did so, they would become the assessed owners and would pay the ordinary taxes on the properties, which, it is suggested in this brief, would be lower than what they are now required to pay.
I think that the final request which the tenants make in their brief to the minister is a very reasonable one. It is this:
On behalf of the Wartime Housing Tenants Association we respectfully urge, Mr. Minister, that you negotiate and conclude an agreement with the city council of Vancouver to have the increased taxation held in abeyance until such time as the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are prepared to have these houses properly appraised and1 a purchase plan submitted to the tenants.
I would ask the minister to answer my two questions: first, why did Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation step in and make a deal with the city over the heads of the tenants; second, what is the reaction of the minister to this request made by the tenants for a proper appraisal and a purchase plan so that they will at least have the option of buying the houses and becoming taxpayers in the ordinary way?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I am surprised at the notice sent out by Central Mortgage, which does not represent the true situation. The houses in Vancouver were built under an agreement with the city in the ordinary way. The land

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
was transferred by the city to the crown, the federal government, and the houses were built. The initial rentals were worked out on the basis of an agreement with the city which provided the usual terms, that we should pay from $22 to $26 a year in taxes to the city, and that the rental would be based on the cost of the project, plus taxes provided for in the agreement. However, the city, as my hon. friend knows, has the right to tax tenants of rented property. It exercises that right quite freely in British Columbia. What actually happened was that the city exercised that right by agreement with the department of municipal affairs of the province. We said that we would collect the tax which the city assessed, provided that we consider the tax reasonable in amount. We thought the tax imposed by the city was reasonable, and we agreed to collect the taxes. It was simply a matter of co-operation. We did not agree to the taxes being imposed. The only part this government had in it was that we said we would collect the taxes for the city if in our opinion the tax was reasonable.
Was any order obtained from the respective tenants authorizing the dominion government to take out that amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No; the city imposed the tax.
Was any authority given by the tenants to the government to pay that amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No; we are simply acting as tax collectors for the city in that regard.
If the tenant did not pay, the city would have to sue.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
It might have been much better to let the city collect the tax from the tenants. Then the matter would have been brought to a head, and I doubt very much whether the city would have tried to collect.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
That may be so. The city had the legal right to impose the tax. The tax was legally imposed, and if we choose to collect it, we do so simply as a matter of co-operation. We try to co-operate with the cities in which we have houses. We did that in this case. We are doing it in every similar case across Canada. If the tax is legally imposed, and we think it not unreasonable, we co-operate with the city by collecting it from the tenants. If the tenant refuses to pay the tax, but is willing to pay the rent, it then becomes a matter between the city and the tenant.
With regard to the second part of the question, about selling the houses, we sell houses wherever the city permits us to do so. The houses were built under an agreement with the city which did not provide for the sale. Many municipalities and cities have released us from that agreement. For instance, the town of North Vancouver released us from the agreement, and we are selling the houses there to veterans. I think we have sold eighty per cent of all the houses we owned in North Vancouver. The former tenant is now the owner, and the city collects the taxes in the ordinary way. The difficulty in Vancouver has been that we have not yet been able to work out a price for land at a level which we believe should be included in the sale price. My hon. friend will understand that. While the city transferred the property to the crown for a dollar a year, there was an agreement that if the property was sold, the city would recover a reasonable price for the land.
Many houses are involved in that transaction. Is it not possible to reach finality on the purchase price and the terms of sale?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It has not been so far. We think we are pretty close to it in Vancouver.
How long have negotiations been going on concerning these prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: About eighteen months.
What proportion of the $50,000,000 is allocated to the construction of wartime housing in rural areas as distinct from towns and cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Wartime housing is not built in rural areas under the usual terms, for reasons that I think my hon. friend will understand. The farm section of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act has been applied to farming areas. In other words, people in the rural areas can borrow money under the National Housing Act to build houses, but houses are not built for rent in rural areas.
What proportion of the total amount invested by government in housing has been spent in urban areas as distinct from rural areas?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The direct investments in housing have all been made in urban areas. Government ownership of houses for rent is confined to urban areas, for reasons that I think my hon. friend will understand. The government has built houses in mining and logging areas by arrangement with the mine owners and others, where the industry has guaranteed

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
the rentals for a period. Ordinarily the government does not build houses for rent in rural areas.

I took this matter up once with the minister, but we came to the end of the session and I did not get the answers. I understand that a large percentage of amounts invested by government in shelter for the people has gone into urban dwellings, and in consequence into shelter for the industrial population. I was endeavouring to find out from the minister what proportion of our total production is sold abroad, and how much greater it is than before the war. I understood that before the war it was somewhere around 35 per cent, and that it would have to be much greater than that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The proportion of our total production is about 35 per cent.
In the United States it is six per cent or seven per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Something less than ten per cent. My hon. friend will realize that the bulk of our exports is in the form of wheat and wheat products, newsprint, forest products and metals. In other words, the vast bulk of our exports is in raw materials. I doubt whether the bulk of our manufactured goods exported is larger in proportion than similar goods from the United States.

It appears that any further houses which are to be built under the wartime housing project, now administered by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, are to cost the tenants a great deal more in rents than some of the houses built previously. In the city from which I come, a two-bedroom house, without basement, now rents for $22. Under the arrangement which we have just been discussing, they will cost the tenant approximately $25. In the negotiations recently carried on with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the city has been informed that in the future it will only be possible to construct two-bedroom houses, without basements, owing to the greatly increased costs. In other words a two-bedroom house with basement, or a three-bedroom house, is right out of the picture. Even the two-bedroom house, without basement, on account of the increased cost, will result in a rental of $37.50 a month to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. On top of that, the city has to impose an amount for taxes which, let us say, will be another $3 or $4 a month-or does the rental include that?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

The minister says that the rental includes the city's taxation for services. We shall then have houses already built and occupied, with rent and taxes charged, renting at $25 a month, with new houses of exactly the same type at $37.50 a month. It seems to me that this will be regarded by tenants, and with some justification, as unfair. Would it not be possible for the dominion government, under these extraordinary circumstances, to absorb some of the cost of construction, or amortize the collection over a longer period, so that the tenants of the two houses virtually side by side W'ould be paying the same rent, instead of a rent of $12.50 more in one case than in the other for exactly the same house? Could not something be done there?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: If my hon. friend had built a house in 1942. the cost would have been a certain figure. If he had built it in 1948, the cost would have been eighty or ninety per cent more. The government is in exactly the same position. The government cannot perform miracles. A reasonable rental for a house built in 1942 would not represent a reasonable rental for a house built in 1948.
Could the minister not amortize it over a longer period?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: WTe are doing that. We are doing everything we ean to hold the line. It will be noticed that whereas the cost has gone up eighty or ninety per cent, rents have gone up about only fifty per cent.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Which is not too bad. To do that we have had to lengthen the time of amortization, lower the cost of the money, and make several moves which are getting us closer to subsidization than-
Why not go the whole way?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is a limit to where we want to go. We are holding the costs as best we can. We put a ceiling on the rentals at $37.50, and if we cannot build in a town, cannot build houses which can rent on the new formula-and that includes $70 to $80 a year in taxes to the municipality, which were not included, I may say, in the early houses-if we cannot build houses to rent at that maximum, then we do not build them. We think we must draw the line on what constitutes low-rental housing, and we believe that today $37.50 does represent low-rental housing in most of the cities of Canada.

In view of the fact that this whole matter w'as discussed when the

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
minister's bill was before the house, although I am not satisfied with the policy he has indicated I will not deal with it any further. However, I wish to ask about another matter in connection with wartime housing, I refer to those projects where arrangements have been made to sell properties to tenants. I have had complaints which I have raised in the house earlier, one being in connection with one of the projects in Montreal. The complaint was that the tenants were virtually being forced to buy alternative accommodation. I had a similar complaint from Fort William. The answer given by the minister was that nobody was being forced to vacate. While that is technically true, the answer is that the tenant is told, "If you are not prepared to buy this house you are now in, you will have to move into a similar house". Is that the policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
Move only once.

An hon. gentleman says, "Move only once". There was no assurance of that. Some of the officials, I am told, told the wives-not the husbands-and said, "You might as well buy your house now, because if you don't, you will have to move, and if you are not willing to buy that one you will have to move again. Why not settle the thing and buy now?" I have information with reference to the project in Fort William. I understand that one of the tenants there said -and this was in March or April: "No. My lease says I can rent this house, and I stand on my rights and will continue to rent. I will not buy this one nor will I move to another". He was told, "In that event we terminate your lease and you will be considered as an overholding and illegal tenant." Is the minister aware of that situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Oh, yes.
That is the case of a man who is to be evicted. How can you say there will be no evictions under this program to sell houses? The two are not consistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The tenants have been enjoying low rent for a number of years.
Under a lease entered into with you.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
But not a long-term lease; a lease from month to month. The tenant has no leasehold right whatever, being a month-to-month tenant. In disposing of these properties, it is quite in order to sell the more desirable houses first. The worst that has happened to any tenant is that he has 5849-350J
been asked to move into a similar house in a different location. Not only that; the cost of moving is compensated to the tenant to the extent of $15. There is no hardship involved, and there is little complaint from the tenants. My hon. friend is going a long way from home when he takes over the work of the hon. member for Fort William, who has been cooperative in working out this situation.

That is an interesting
observation on the part of the minister. At Kamloops, I may say, these houses are not yet being sold. I am glad the minister appreciates the co-operation of the member for Fort William, but I can tell him that when I was in Fort William I was sought out by a group of tenants who brought their complaints to me, and also showed me a little pamphlet put out by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation last July. The pamphlet contained a series of questions and answers. The first question reads:
If the present tenant does not wish to purchase the house in which he is living, will he be asked to vacate?
The answer is:
It is not the intention of Wartime Housing Limited to disturb any tenant at the time houses are offered for sale. However, a tenant is expected to live up to requirements of his rental lease, making payments on or before due date and taking proper care of the property.
That is the only requirement that is laid down. It States that it is not the intention of Wartime Housing Limited to disturb any tenant at the time houses are offered for sale. This means: So long as you continue to make your payments regularly, and to maintain the property, you will not be turned out.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It does not say that at all.
It is not the intention to disturb any tenant at the time of making sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It does not say, "at the time of making sale".
At the- time houses are offered for sale.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.
That is what is going on.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Sales have been actually -made.
Yes, and the tenant, when his house is offered- for sale, is required to buy or to move to another one. That involves a great deal of disturbance.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
Don't read into it something that it does not say.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

I did no such thing. I said that the only meaning that could be taken from these words is exactly what they say: thait when these houses are offered for sale it is not intended to disturb any tenant, and the orily way of avoiding 'disturbance of the tenant is not to move him. But you are moving him.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend knows very much about the situation.
Of course I dio not hold myself up as an expert, but I think I can understand the plain meaning of words, and the meaning I have ascribed to these words is the meaning they bear.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Let me ask my hon. friend this question. What does it mean when it says the tenant will not be disturbed- when the house is offered for sale-that is, when it is advertised for sale?
It means that the tenant will not be required to move.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is one thing to offer the houses for sale -and another thing to close the sale.
Is this intended to fool the tenant?
A play on words to fool him.
Whait is the meaning of the other words, that a tenant is expected to live up to requirements of his rental lease? What is the meaning of those two sentences placed side by side?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Read the other nine clauses and you will get to the one that is pertinent.

I have already read all -the other clauses. The second question is: "Who has first opportunity to purchase a house?" and the answer to that question is: "Tenant now occupying the house." Read that in conjunction with No. 1 and you will see that the obvious intention is: If you don't wish to purchase, you will not be disturbed.
Mr. HO-WE: You are reading there something that I do not find in print.

It states that it is not intended to disturb any tenant "at the time houses are -offered for sale". It does not say at the time his house is being offered for sale, but at the time houses are being offered for sale. But tenants are being disturbed, and the obvious intention is not being carried out. There is a change in policy. Here is a letter from the minister addressed to a tenant of

the Montreal project on March 2 in which he himself admits that hardship will be imposed on tenants. He says in part:
. . . we intend to proceed as planned.
That is, with this sale and the moving of tenants.
We realize that circumstances will arise where even alternate accommodation within the same project wall impose hardship upon the tenant being asked to move.
It certainly cannot be maintained that the first position held ou-t in this pamphlet is being followed, and that hardship is not being imposed on tenants who are asked to move. I would ask that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation revert to their plan as put out in this pamphlet, and that the tenant who is unable to buy the house when offered for sale be not required to move.
I conclude by drawing the minister's attention to this. These tenants in many cases have put in special work on their houses. They have made gardens and have had fixtures installed and they do not wish to move to some other place that has not a garden.
Why don't they buy them?

Because they cannot afford to, as the hon. member for Vancouver North knows. Many of these tenants cannot afford to buy at the time houses are offered for sale.
Mr. H-OWE:	The man is a munitions
worker. He moved into one of these houses in 1942 or 1943 because the rent was favourable and we were anxious to get him there. We needed his work in a particular plant. Does he think that the fact that he moved there in 1942 should guarantee him occupancy of the house for life? Is that the- thought of my hon. friend? What divine right has he to have greatly preferred rentals for life just because he happened to move into a house in ,1942? Why should he not buy?

The minister asks what divine right a tenant has to stay in a house into which 'he moved during the war. I do not intend to answer that question in the way in which it should be answered, but I will say this without going into a theological argument. The tenants in many cases, as they have themselves told -me, were asked to go there. The minister himself has admitted that they were anxious to get these men to go to work in the munitions factories, in the tank building or gun- building factories and so on. So they said to them, "If you will come and work in our factories, we will give you low-rental houses". They went in there on those undertakings and they are continuing to work in the same plant.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Very few of them.

The ones I have spoken to. It is peculiar that the minister and I do not seem to see the same people or the same set of circumstances, especially when it comes so close to his own home. But the ones I have spoken to are continuing to work there. They tell me that they have moved there, in some cases from great distances, admittedly partly because an attractive job was offered to them, but also because the government said, "We need you here and we will provide you with accommodation". So, having assessed the need, they perhaps changed markedly their whole course of life. They moved from the prairies to Fort William or to Montreal or from Vancouver to the prairies, or vice versa, with their families. Having sized up the situation they said, "We are going to make this move and stay here". Certainly nothing was told them at the time to indicate that some months or some years later they would be required to buy or to leave the houses in which they were settled. I do not think even the minister, with all the power he has, can confer a divine right on himself or any tenant. But I certainly think the tenants were given the understanding that they would be permitted to enjoy possession of the property so long as they continued to pay their rent promptly.

I should like to say a few words following what the hon. member for Kamloops has just said. I will speak only about my own riding of Vancouver North in which we had one of the first and largest wartime housing projects in order to provide, as the minister has pointed out, cheap available rental accommodation for the men who worked in the shipyards.
Instead of criticizing the ministry at this time-and I think I do my share of that-I wish heartily to commend Wartime Housing for the job they did during the war and for the job they have done since. In my own riding the great bulk of the people were anxious to buy these houses. We had two years of difficulty with a city administration; and in the end it was necessary to change the city administration over this one issue. But, although sales have been going on for only three months, the contractors say the people of North Vancouver have gladly picked up these wartime houses. They want to buy the houses.
I wish to tell the hon. member for Kamloops that it is precisely those people who have done something to their houses-who have built fences, put in nice gardens and electric fixtures-who are the ones who are so anxious to buy. When you see the wartime
housing development, you see a fairly good cross-section of human nature. Every house on the North Vancouver property started out the same, and the people moved in. Some took the finest care of their homes and made those little wartime houses as attractive as any in North Vancouver. Other people drawing the same wages on the same job, moved into these houses just as the builders left them; and now five years later the houses are still the same way. Those are the people who-
Those are the people who have an opportunity to buy a better house.
No.
Yes.

The people who are able to buy better houses are already buying houses. The hon. member for Kamloops was talking about divine right. These people think it is their divine right because they worked in the shipyards during the war.
I was not talking about divine right. The minister was.

My hon. friend was
talking about a theological argument.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I suppose my hon. friend does not know the meaning of the words he is using. He was saying he did not want to get involved in a theological argument. However, these people are the very ones who think that now they should be allowed to continue to get these houses for $25 a month, despite the fact that there are over three hundred married veterans in North Vancouver, men who fought overseas, who are most anxious to get into these houses. I do not know about Fort William or Montreal. I just know about my own riding, and I had a considerable amount to do with the negotiations. The people of North Vancouver as a whole are glad to see that these houses at last are paying their proper share of the tax burden; and the people in the houses are now glad to be, as they themselves describe it, not second-class citizens getting a free ride at the expense of the people of North Vancouver through just paying $25 taxes instead of $100. The same situation applies in the city of Vancouver, as the hon. member for Vancouver South knows. The only criticism I have heard-
They are nearly all veterans there.

That is quite right.
North Vancouver was not a veterans project.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
But a veteran has been put in every house that has become vacant. Today there are over three hundred overseas veterans with two or more children, who were resident on the north shore before enlistment and who are anxious to get in to buy these houses, and I say they should have that right.
In North Vancouver the only criticism with regard to this plan was that it was not consummated two years ago. Even many of the shipyard workers have complained to me that they have been paying rentals which should have been going toward capital payment for the last two years, because of the failure not of Wartime Housing but of civic administration-the mayor at that time-to consummate the deal. I should like to commend the minister in this matter, and I think they could well afford to build even more of this type of housing for the veterans in the Vancouver area.

I think I know something
about wartime housing in Fort William. The first criticism was that the government was extravagant in building these houses in the first place, that in the first year after the war they would be pulled to pieces, and that this would be the fault of the government. Now these, houses are worth more than they were then.
Prices have gone up.

I saw a number of people who came to me wanting an opportunity of buying these houses because of their associations. Some of them made some improvements. But when a young veteran and a young mother live in a home, and a little happy coal oil stove comes into it to light it up. you can see that there is an association in that home that is fine. It was my urgent plea to the minister and Wartime Housing to give to those people who wanted it an opportunity to buy those houses. In Fort William we have people who own houses thej' moved into as war workers and who never owned a home before; and I have commended several of them for it.
I know some people were not satisfied. They said, when the agent called on them during the daytime, he should not have called then but should have called at night. It was impossible for agents to make all these calls in the evening. I placed all the different arguments and discontents before the minister; and if hon. members want to see a fine bit of literature, with arguments thoroughly answered to the satisfaction of a great many people in Fort William, with the exception perhaps of one or two, I say they

should get from the minister's office a copy of that brief. I commend the minister for his generosity and for his outstanding patience with regard to this matter of wartime housing.

I want to answer some of the comments that have been made by the hon. member for Vancouver North, because I am not speaking against the tenant who wishes to buy his home being allowed to do so. I agree that he should be not only permitted but encouraged to buy his own home if he is in a position to do so. My point is that the tenant who is not in a position to buy at the moment or who does not wish to buy the house should not be forced to move because somebody else from some other house in the project wishes to buy the particular house which this tenant is in.
The hon. member for Vancouver North spoke as though all tenants were in a position to buy the houses they are living in and there would be no hardship done. I want to read him an extract from a letter I have received from the tenant of a house in one of these projects which were thrown open for sale; this is from the wife of the tenant. They did not wish to buy, and the agent of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation came around to call on them and said they had from somebody else an offer to purchase the house these tenants were in. She went on to say:
He then went on bo tell us that seeing as we are on a corner lot, and have cupboard doors on our cupboards in the kitchen-

We put the actual figures of the steel plant at Sault Ste. Marie on the record. These figures showed that, despite the fact that wages were increased by 25 per cent, because of increased production during the same period the increased wage cost was completely offset. Last evening the hon. member for Calgary West made the observation that in my own union, the miners' union of Nova Scotia, the answer was increased production to offset the increased wage cost. In answer to the indignant statement of the hon. member for Lake Centre-
I do not think we are all dishonest, as my hon. friends to the left suggest.

I will not generalize, but my hon. friend the member for Lake Centre will remember this. A statute was passed early in 1939 limiting profits to five per cent on all war contracts and when this house met in September, 1939, the present minister was questioned as to why that profit limitation in war contracts was removed by order in council. His answer at that time, as I remember it, and I am speaking from memory, was to this effect, that for months he had tried to let war contracts for industry but he could find no one to accept a war contract until such time as that profit limitation was removed. That is when/ Britain had her back to the wall, and that does not suggest that patriotism took precedence over profits even in the dark days of 1940.
I said a moment ago I was speaking from memory. The statement will be found in Hansard of September 12, 1939, at page 179:
The provision of 5 per cent was put in the last act . after a good deal of consideration as a minimum return for the service rendered, but it was one which men of considerable experience believed to be unworkable. I can say to my hon. friend that from that day to this the defence purchasing board has done its very best to place contracts on that basis and has used every pressure that could be brought to bear in the form of patriotism and so on, but to date it has not succeeded in placing a single contract on that basis.
What is the date of that?
September 12, 1939.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend describes that as though the limitation-
Three days after the war began.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: -were five per cent on cost. It was not five per cent on cost. It was five per cent on the money invested in the productive equipment. It was worded-
September 12, 1939, was three or four days after the war began. Therefore no contracts had been let as yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I know. But it described events in the period of some seven or eight months between the passage of the legislation and the date when I was speaking. The actual profits in the munitions works were nearer two per cent. I think the average

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
profits throughout the war averaged about two per cent. But that two per cent profit is two per cent on the value of the product. The five per cent that my hon. friend was talking about had nothing to do with the value of the product. It had to do with the capital invested, which is quite different and quite unworkable. It was devised by our friends in the east block without a great deal of knowledge of the productive problems.
That is a good admission.

I should just like to get this fact on the record. The hon. member for Cape Breton South stated, if I understood him correctly, that eighty per cent of the cost-plus contracts during the war were dealt with dishonestly.

No. I refuse, Mr. Chairman, to allow the hon. member to put words into my mouth. I said that if the hon. member who was questioning me at that time would question the minister and his officials, they would likely inform him that eighty per cent of the contracts operated on a cost-plus basis during the war militated against the best interests of this country from the standpoint of spending money. I did not say anything about dishonesty, and I do not intend to let the hon. member put words into my mouth. My hon. friends over here to my right can become as indignant as they like. That statement of mine still stands. If any of them have any evidence to the contrary, let them put it on the record here.
Have you any evidence to that effect?

I am reasonably sure. I tell my hon. friends to talk with their own members on the war expenditures committee. I say to them to go and talk to some of those who were probing those cost-plus contracts. I have had members of their group show me evidence which they wanted me to use, but which I thought was too rotten to use. I am quite willing to face facts and be honest about these things. But when the hon. member for Stanstead gets up in this house and tries to put words into my mouth, that is something I will not stand for. My statement is on the record that these contracts militated against the best interests of this country from the financial standpoint; and all the evidence given to the war expenditures committee will bear that out. Profits were placed above patriotism when this world was in a bad state, on the removal of that five per cent profit limitation. That is my interpretation of it.
I was interrupted by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. We will take his restatement.
It is not a restatement at all. That is the first statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

We will take the last statement of the hon. member for Cape Breton South as being the statement by which he wishes to stand. The allegation is that eighty per cent of the cost-plus contracts were carried out in a way that was prejudicial to the interests of Canada. Then, in support of his charge he reads a statement that was made to the house on some day early in September.
September 12, 1939.

Yes. War was declared on September 10, 1939. The hon. member for Cape Breton South is relying upon a statement that was made in the house two days after war was declared as proof that eighty per cent of the cost-plus contracts were carried out in a way that was prejudicial to the interests of Canada.
That is plain nonsense.
Those are the facts.
No.
I merely wish that they appear in sequence in the record.
That is just plain nonsense.

I think the facts are that there were not in Canada any big interests or any capitalists in 1939 who were more than five per cent patriotic; that is to say, they said they could make five per cent on their capital, but that was not enough for them. They were not patriotic enough to accept that.
Oh, oh.
That is the story the minister himself has acknowledged.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is no occasion for my hon. friend to make twisting speeches. I said nothing of the kind.
What did you say?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I said that the basis or the provision of the act was not workable. The provision was for a maximum return of five per cent on the capital involved in the particular operation. In the first place, it was exceedingly difficult to allocate the capital involved in the particular operation. In the second place, no one dared to take a contract because the terms were so vague as to the limitation.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I do not think I have twisted it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: People use the five per cent limitation quite loosely. It needs to be carefully defined.

While I am on my feet, I also wish to say that I should like the minister to be a little bit more consistent. With respect to subsidies he has just said that as soon as you introduce a subsidy you discourage incentive. I assume that is true. But in the very item before this he has given $370,000 as an incentive bonus to industry. If subsidies are to be taken as destroying incentive, why should the people of Canada pay taxes to destroy incentive, as evidently it would do?

Here, Mr. Chairman, is a member of a party which, long after the war had started, advocated not sending any troops to help dear old Britain with her back to the wall; they said to keep the men in Canada to defend the worlds-keep them right here; make Canada the battlefield. That is what they advocated during the war. Now they are trying to create class hatred more than ever by saying of a man who allowed his factory to be used on a common-sense, reasonable basis for the purpose of making munitions of war that he gouged the public, and that, unless he was paid blood money, he would not have put forth any effort on behalf of the war.
That is correct.
That is what is being expounded here today by the group which, on the whole, advocated keeping their sons right in this country and not fighting for the British empire. I say, shame on you.
May I ask the hon. member for Simcoe North if his speech was prepared by the hon. member for Vancouver East?
I have never been fortunate enough to have anyone prepare my speeches for me.

I think we might leave it at this, that if Canada got good value for the money spent during the war, in connection with war production, we got it because we had good inspection. I have had something to do with contracts, in a small way, in the city of Vancouver, and I was told that the value we got from the contractors in any contract work that was let was just as good as the inspection, and no better. If the inspection was poor, the value received was poor. If the inspection

was good, the value received was good. And if we will throw our minds back to the first world war we will remember that paper-soled shoes were sold to the troops; we will remember that bacon was filled with brine and fed to the troops; we will remember that beef was embalmed and fed to the troops. I do not suppose we have improved morally veiy much from 1914-18 to 1939-45.

I think it is very unfortunate that if, as has been suggested here, there are five per cent of business concerns whose morals are not 100 per cent perfect, their lapses of moral turpitude should always be quoted by the C.C.F. That does not prove anything so far as the free enterprise system is concerned. I am confident if I had to depend upon hon. members opposite to produce very much, either in war or in peace, we would not have much wealth in this country at any time.
I just wish to add a word. There are times in this house when I am impressed by the sincerity, and sometimes even by the logic, of those to my left. But when they get down to smearing-
Who started it?

You did. When they get down to this smearing of business, and trying to create the impression that except in the rarest of cases, which we all despise, there is any concerted attempt on the part of business to deal unfairly, I resent it. The hon. member for Vancouver East, under the guise of dealing fairly with the matter, said the goods received were only as good as the inspection.
I do not care whether you resent it or not; it is the truth.
I think it is unfair, and I think that kind of smear campaign will get them nowhere.

The
reason the minister indicated for the increased cost of steel and iron products was the increase in the cost of scrap metal. Can the minister tell the committee what amount, if any, has been exported to other countries in the last five years, and to what countries such exports were made?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
There has been a prohibition against the export of steel scrap, except for an occasional swap. I think a little steel was exchanged on the Pacific coast. Canadian scrap delivered to Seattle against Buffalo scrap moving to Hamilton, the reason being to save

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
freight charges. But, other than that, on balance Canada has been an importer of scrap and has not permitted exports.

speechtext:
Item agreed to.
hi7. Administration, reconversion and operation of Canadian Arsenals Limited, $2,900,000.
How much did we spend under this item in 1947-48?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: This represents the difference between the cost of administering all government arsenals, which is $4,400,000, and the estimated earnings of about $1,500,000.

What would be the
amount allocated' to reconversion?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think the reconversion work at the arsenals is pretty well finished.
My point is that there would always be more or less of an amount for conversion. It would always be changing to a certain extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes.

I was wondering why this was put in. I should think it would be more accurate to say that this amount was for administration and operation. Would there not always be conversion going on in connection with the making of munitions?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Perhaps so. The hon. member will understand that when the war ended we allocated certain war plants as arsenals. I believe we have seven or eight arsenal plants. We moved into those plants machinery from others sufficient to make it possible for the arsenals to make anything made during the war. There was a good deal of expense attached to that operation. Some of (his money may be used for that purpose. In any event, it is the total expenditure estimated to maintain the arsenals, less earnings.
Is the production entirely for government use, or are sales made to the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: We make sales as we can. The countries to whom we can make sales are rather limited. However, we have made sales occasionally from the aresnals.
What amounts are required to maintain the other crown companies? I have in mind the Eldorado Mining and Refining Company and the Polymer Corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Eldorado Mining and Refining is healthy. Operating profits for the twelve months ended March 31, 1948, amounted to $1,087,318.97.
What about Polymer?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Polymer made its depreciation, plus about $25,000.
How many crown companies have been brought into existence since the war? The minister told us last night that all but five had ceased to do business; but there have been some new ones since.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The Canadian Commercial
Corporation was brought into being to take over the purchasing functions of the Department of Munitions and Supply. The Export Credits Insurance Corporation, which was incorporated by act of parliament a year or two ago, is another one. They are the only two I can remember.
Were there any others?
Would the minister inform me-
I was in the middle of a question.
Would the minister inform me under whose advice the arsenal was constructed at Kamloops, where it is subject to flooding?
What arsenal are you talking about?
Munitions stored in that area.
That is different from an arsenal.
All right; munitions storage depot. On whose advice was it constructed and who is in charge? What military command advised the construction at that spot?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Obviously the hon. member must ask that question of the Minister of National Defence. I am not aware of the details. All I know is that the Department of National Defence chose the location and ordered the construction there.
That answer partly satisfies me.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: It is not an arsenal. It is a storage dump belonging to the armed forces.
Yes, but obviously it was constructed on somebody's advice. I should like to know, through you, who advised its construction in its present location.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The Minister of National Defence will be in the house next week and

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
will be prepared to answer all questions. I suggest that the hon. member ask him that question.
Are there any other crown corporations apart from the two which are under the administration of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There are statutory crown companies; I suppose you could call the Canadian National Railways a crown company. We had some thirty crown companies during the war, but today only four are left. By crown company I mean a company operating under the Companies Act. There are other crown companies set up by statute, which are in a different category. I have mentioned two connected with the department with which I am associated, but there may be others of that type. I think we now have only four which had been set up under the Companies Act.
Does the minister know of any other companies, apart from the two under his administration, which have been set up since the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No.
What was the total production of Polymer during the year ended March 31? How much was deducted by way of depreciation, or at what amount was depreciation computed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The net profit for the year's operation was $25,623, after provision was made for $2,192,967 for depreciation of plant and equipment.
What is the value of the plant and equipment today?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think it stands on the books at about $38,000,000; that is the net total cost of the plant, less repayment of capital from operating profits. The value of the production was $17,000,000.

I read in the press that the manager had been abroad in an effort to get markets in Europe for the production of Polymer. To what extent did he succeed, and what were the values of the exports during the year ending March 31?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The trip was successful. For instance, he sold the entire requirements of the Michelin company of France for butyl rubber to be used for inner tubes. The Michelin company ship crude rubber of an equivalent value to New York. It is sold for United States funds which are applied against the purchase of butyl rubber at Sarnia. The exports of G.R.S. rubber were 11,784,000 pounds to the Reconstruction Finance Cor-

poration and 21,392,000 pounds to other importers. Exports of butyl rubber were 95,000 pounds to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, and 2,379,000 pounds to other export buyers.
Can Polymer compete with natural rubber?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I think Polymer has had its worst year last year. The price of natural rubber dropped to below fourteen cents and, in order to hold its customers, Polymer had to drop its price to fifteen cents a pound, which is very close to production cost. Later, the price of natural rubber moved back to around twenty to twenty-five cents a pound, and Polymer advanced its price to eighteen and nineteen cents a pound. During the period the price was at fifteen cents, the corporation was operating very close to the red ink.
What salary is paid the chief executive?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Twenty-five thousand dollars a year.

____________Supply-Reconstruction and Supply

speechtext: Yes, one small company to handle patents. There was no machinery for the marketing of patents which had been taken out by employees in the national research council or workers in the universities in the name of the government. Most other countries have patent corporations. The advantage of having a patent corporation is that it provides not only marketing facilities for Canadian patents but permits agency arrangements in connection with patents originating in the United States or the United Kingdom which can be offered to the market in Canada. All patents owned by the government have been transferred to this corporation, and it has made some marketing arrangements of considerable advantage.

How does the national
research council come into the picture?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: By arrangement between the governments, patents held by a similar corporation in the United States are made available to Canadian users through the Canadian Patent Corporation. In other words, they can apply through the corporation for Canadian rights to United States patents.
Private firms?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: That is right. The purpose of the corporation is to sell public patents to private firms.
In Canada and abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: This corporation works with corresponding corporations in other countries. For instance, our Canadian patents will be listed with the United States and the British government corporations. If there is no appropriate corporation to handle patents abroad they can be sold from Canada, but it is believed that in handling publicly owned patents it is better to work through government corporations.

Are these patents that recently originated in Canada, or are they patents that have become public property by reason of the activities of the custodian of alien enemy property? There were a great many German patents registered here, and I assume that the custodian had a vested right in them for a time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The purpose of the corporation is to market patents taken out by government employees in the name of the crown. I cannot say whether the corporation has taken over the German patents that were lodged with the custodian. There was some talk of their doing so, but whether it was actually done or not I
cannot say. That will be between the national research council and the patent office.

friend knows that the rules are that the committee deals with the item before it, but if he wishes to ask for the consent of the committee to go back to a certain item-
