speechtext:
Item agreed to.
JiO'i. Administration expenses of the atomic energy control board, $77,272.

This and the next two items have to do with the atomic energy control board, and I think it would be appropriate if the minister would make a statement concerning the activities of that board. As he knows the house has had very little opportunity to find out just what is being done by the board, and this is the occasion when we should have an explanation.
There is one other point in connection with the board. When the bill was passed in 1946 there was agreement, I think on all sides of the house, that theTe should be a watchdog committee, similar to the committee in the United States where they have nine members of the senate and nine members of the house of representatives constituting a committee on atomic energy. At that time, in 1946, the present minister took this position, which will be found at page 2401 of Hansard of that year:
Then my hon. friend mentioned watchdog committees.
In opening the debate, I had suggested that there should be watchdog committees, one of which would be composed of members of the Senate and members of the House of Commons. As I have explained, that was supported by several members from each of the parties. I continue:
I dare say that, as developments proceed, it may be desirable to have committees, and perhaps a standing committee of this house on problems of atomic energy may be warranted; I do not think that is so at the moment. We should obtain more experience in the work of atomic energy before a standing committee is established. But that may very well be a logical development of the future if and when atomic energy takes a more important place in the Canadian economy. There is nothing in the bill that wrould prevent the establishing of advisory committees or the setting up of a parliamentary committee, should the future indicate that that is desirable.
Two years have gone by. Last year the minister explained to the house that the work

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
being done in Canada on atomic energy had to do with the use for civilian purposes, and not for war purposes, which I suggest removes some of the need for secrecy; that was the main basis on which this house was refused any hand whatsoever in the development of atomic energy back in 1946. I suggest to hon. members that atomic energy may be of the utmost importance in the economic life of Canada in the years that lie ahead. We all hope that it will be.
It is an unsound position that on this question this house should be working entirely in the dark. We know absolutely nothing of what the possibilities are, or what progress has been made. I do not think that condition exists with regard to any other activity of government. Here we have a board operating without any real control by parliament, and without parliament having any knowledge of what is being done. The board is not even a fulltime board; it is more or less of an honorary board; the chairman has other duties which take up most of his time. I suggest that the time has now come when there should be set up some sort of parliamentary committee on atomic energy. If that cannot be done, then parliament should be given some more direct control over the activities of the atomic energy control board.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I had expected that this subject would come up earlier in the session, and I had gone to the trouble of preparing a brief but eloquent speech, telling about everything that Canada is doing on atomic energy. Perhaps I can dig out of the speech about as much as I can read from now until six o'clock, and give an idea of what we are doing, and after that we can discuss the other problem.
I should like to hear the minister give us the whole story.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I would love to, but time
moves on.
Put it on the record.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: No.
It is of great importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: An undelivered speech is a great asset. Perhaps if the committee does not want it I might deliver it at some other forum.
I should like to hear it all.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I shall start from the point that tells what we are doing at the moment at Chalk River; that is, the peacetime use. I could hold in my hand a small cylinder of
natural metallic uranium. The cylinder I had prepared for this demonstration was about the size of the little jack-knife I now hold in my hand. We now know that if every bit of this very heavy metal could be turned into energy -which theoretically it can be-we would get the same quantity of power that could be developed by about 500,000 tons of coal, or about the power we now get out of the large Shipshaw plant in one year. There is little doubt that some day we shall be able to fly to remote areas, in one small aeroplane, more potential power in the form of nuclear fuel than can be hauled today in a hundred railway coal cars. One does not require an extraordinary imagination to envisage what that may mean to future developments. But as I have said, there are many problems to be solved before commercial atomic power is an economic reality. Our Chalk River plant is working vigorously on the fundamental problems involved, and we are keeping in as close touch as possible with what is going on in other countries.
While commercial atomic power is definitely not "just around the corner", there are immediate dividends in connection with radioactive isotopes and their use in medicine, biological research, and industrial applications, which I shall mention in a few moments and which some people feel may ultimately yield greater and more significant returns than all the conceivable applications of ordinary power.
Now, as to what we are doing at the moment at Chalk River. The pile is running satisfactorily; plutonium is being made in the rods; but, since it takes some time to build up that material in the rods, the chemical extraction plant is not yet functioning, although extraction on a laboratory scale is being carried on. We are producing, using, and distributing, a series of radio-isotopes, and the research and engineering staffs are extremely busy on an extensive series of investigations on the chemical, biological, medical and industrial uses of isotopes. Also fundamental nuclear investigations on the effect of radiation on structural material are being carried on, which are necessary before commercial atomic energy plants can become a practical economic reality.
It might seem that, since we are now running a pile or nuclear furnace which gives off heat, it should be easy to develop power on a commercial basis. It is true that the Chalk River plant is now discharging into the river hot water which might be used to heat buildings. This could be done, of course, but the temperatures are so low that it would cost more than it does by the use of conventional steam heating. This is not because higher temperatures cannot be produced; but because,

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
at the moment, the structural materials available that will stand high temperatures are unsatisfactory from the standpoint of absorption of neutrons. This means that much research must be done to develop new materials, because unfortunately materials of the engineering standard textbooks are not satisfactory.
We also know little about the effects of intense radiation on structural materials. Here again we have a revolutionary new force that engineers in the past never had to take into account in structural design, and we must accumulate the necessary fundamental facts before we can design high-temperature power reactors with confidence.
In the field of radioactive isotopes, the situation has more immediate promise, and we are now making dozens of different kinds and are regularly distributing to workers in ten universities quantities of thirteen of the most important radio-isotopes such as radioactive phosphorus, sodium, carbon, calcium, iodine, et cetera. In addition, of course, even larger quantities are being used in the national research laboratories at Chalk River and elsewhere.
I think most hon. members realize that radioactive isotopes have three main uses. They are useful as tracers in research and analytical procedures. They hold great promise in the field of medicine for clinical use as a radioactive source, and they have almost limitless possibilities in the broad field of industry for control and other purposes. Perhaps a few examples will be helpful. For instance, iodine is known to concentrate in the thyroid gland; hence, if a compound containing radioactive iodine is given a patient, the course of its path through the body may be traced and the rate of accumulation in the thyroid can be determined by instruments outside the human body which record intensities of radiation. It can be easily seen that in a similar way, where treatment by radiation has proved helpful, it may be possible, in the future, to carry that radiation to the proper tissues by radio-isotopes.
There is siurely an immense field for the use of tracers in research work in chemistry, in biology, and in medicine. In determining just what happens in biological processes, the tracer techniques provide a new wool as potentially novel and useful as was the microscope when first introduced. In the treatment of disease, there is a future so hopeful that many believe the benefits from medical research alone will some day repay manyfold all our considerable expenditures.
I could go on giving scores of examples of the use that is now being made of radio-

isotopes by Canadian scientists, but time will not permit. I do want, however, to say that in the field of agriculture also the experiments being carried out in western Canada have already given most important information about the way in which plants take up elements from fertilizers, where the various nutritional elements in feeds go, and how they are assimilated. It is predicted that the use of tracers will have a profound effect on agricultural science and production.
But perhaps the greatest quantitative use of tracers will be in industry. Even today, isotopes and radiation are being used in scores of industries, in chemical plants, in metallurgy, in textiles, in the oil industry, and in thousands of plants, particularly in the United States, where intensive studies are being made everywhere to see if industrial processes cannot be improved and costs cut down by the use of this new technique. For instance, in mixing chemicals, tracers can indicate accurately how much of each type is in the final product. Again, where raw materials from different parts of the world go into one product and where quality is effected by blending, tracer techniques can provide easily the definite answer wanted as to just how much of each ingredient is in the final product. In metallurgy the uses are obvious and many. In studies of the wear of bearings it has been possible to detect the migration of atoms of metals from one piece to another; information that was heretofore impossible. Also the phenomena of annealing, grain growth, and transformation of one type of iron into another can be closely studied.
Again in control operations, in industries where it is desirable to know the composition of wastes; in dye industries, where it is essential to follow the strength of solutions; in the oil industry, where control is essential; in these and hundreds of other cases, the use of tracers for analytical purposes is proving most useful. In addition, other unsuspected uses for radiation are being worked out, such as the instrument which will follow and chart the internal corrosion of a metal retort or vessel from an external location, the gauge which will record levels of liquids in tanks, and the device which measures and controls the density of solutions in large tanks. There is also a useful device for removing the static from paper and textile machines which has shown real economies. That device is being sold commercially by the government. In fact, so attractive are the potential uses in industry that one might almost say that within two or three years the real initiative and enter-

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
prise of a country's industries will be measured by the use they are making of isotopes and radiation techniques.
From what I have said I hope the committee will appreciate that our enterprise at Chalk River is not an ordinary industrial undertaking which can be judged by the immediate output of plutonium. It is really an exploration expedition into a land of great promise. We have a staff of about 250 scientists and technicians, with an additional 750 employees and, beside the output of isotopes and plutonium, there are now being turned out hundreds of original scientific papers which are rapidly establishing the scientific quality and reputation of this Canadian scientific centre, which even now is a place to which the great scientists of the world come for discussions and information.
While the tangible and immediate results in production, in research, and in development, are impressive and worthwhile, I should like to remind hon. members that the ultimate results of the best research can seldom be immediately discerned. We know by experience that where we have first-rate research in any field, there is almost sure to be an overflow into adjacent fields, and the unexpected harvests are often the most valuable.
In closing, I suggest that this rather large enterprise which we undertook at Chalk River in a time of war is turning out to be an absolutely first-rate effort that will continue in the years to come to be a credit to Canada in every sense.
The minister did not deal with the suggestion that we have a committee of the senate and this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I doubt whether a committee is necessary. Since the work done is chiefly confined to peacetime uses, control is more or less obvious. The work is being laid out by the national research council; the council has its medical committee and men interested in plant research, and other research of various types, and these committees are directing the experimental work that is being carried out.
If a committee of the house wishes to go there and see the work at Chalk River that will be possible. The atomic energy commission has no great decisions to make. We have freed control of material in the ground. Its duties are confined to purchasing fissionable materials after they are mined, and controlling their refining and sale. That today is concerned only with the Eldorado operations. There is no private operation either present or contemplated, which we know of,
although there are rumours of the finding of new deposits of ore. I can think of no reason why any formal board should be set up, but if the house at the next session wished to appoint a committee on atomic energy and bring experts before that committee to discuss these matters it might be appropriate to do so.

Would the minister consider making a move of that kind at the next session? I know that nothing can be done during the present session; but in the intervening months, between now and the session of 1949, perhaps the government could give some thought to the advisability of setting up a committee of the house or a joint committee of the senate and the house.
'Mr, HOWE: I would certainly have no objection to doing that. I would be glad to consider it.
If the hon. member for Vancouver South belonged to such a committee he would turn into a statue of salt.
Is there any oo-operation between the research going on in Canada and that which is taking place in the United States and Britain with respect to atomic energy?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Yes. There is close co-operation.

The minister said that knowledge of atomic energy would be used more particularly in the United States. By that, does he mean that United States industry is using to a greater extent than Canadian industry the knowledge that we also have of atomic energy?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Industry in the United States is about ten or fifteen times the size of industry in Canada, and therefore more people are interested in research, and in the application of atomic energy to industry. Our industry is also active, but there is a larger use in the United States.

Because it is larger, it does not follow that it is more progressive or up to date, or should be, in the use of the technological knowledge which we have. I think attention should be paid to that phase of the matter to see that our Canadian industries utilize the atomic energy knowledge that we have.
Is Canada the principal source of fissionable material for the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: No, not the principal source.

I have seen metals-I believe it is uranium-coming from the Flin Flon deposits. Is there any danger of such metals or ores finding their way

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
into the hands of people who should not have them, in view of the fact that the government has removed the controls in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: My hon. friend has never seen uranium metal.
I do not know. It is an ore.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: He could have seen low-grade ore. But there is no great danger with low-grade ore. The refinement process is a complicated one. The ore is no more dangerous than any other kind of ore. The ore is not fissionable, but it can be made into fissionable material.

items 396 and 397 for the dominion coal board were carried, I believe it was agreed that there would be some further discussion.
rMr. McCullough (Assiniboia).]
I know, Mr. Chairman, that the minister hates to see me get up just as much as I hate to get up.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I would not say that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No. We are glad to see you get up.

I do not intend to take long on the subject. I was anxious that the minister should make some statement on this item, the dominion coal board, because it is a new piece of machinery established nationally to try to do something about developing the Canadian coal industry, and also about developing a national fuel policy in the field of marketing. The coal board itself was appointed as a result of a recommendation of the royal commission, and it has functioned for a year. I thought the minister might have something to say as to how it has worked, what new fields it has opened up or it has in mind with respect to a national fuel policy. That is mainly the reason why I rise at this time.
I shall not talk about what the fuel policy should be, or to any extent about the development of the resources of Canada. I have done that so often in the house that I hate to see myself doing it all over again.
You must be getting fed up with it.

No, not exactly. I think the setting up of the board itself and giving to it the function it has to perform is a step in the right direction. I said that when the board was set up. According to the Financial Post, the board has a scheme under way now for the further mechanization of the coal mines of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Does that paper in the hon. member's party now correspond with the Toronto Globe and Mail in the Progressive Conservative party?

It is rather unfortunate that one picks up in that paper a considerable number of things that we do not get in the house. This issue of it had about eight pages on maritime industry, as to the things that were to be done and the things that the government were doing. Among the items was a fairly comprehensive statement as to the negotiations being carried on between the dominion government and the corporation; and I presume that is the dominion coal board.
Last night the argument with regard to the development of the hard-coal areas in Alberta reminded me of the arguments we were mak-

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
ing twenty years ago along the same lines. The factor that has always prevented the development of the Canadian industry has, in my opinion, been the question of markets. The coal is east and west and our main market is in the centre of Canada. In that respect you were bucking geography. I always contended that the only way to overcome it was to zone the markets in Canada that were as economic as possible. Then, your subvention arrangement would enable our coal from the east and1 west to go into the markets as far to the centre of Canada as possible and compete, with government assistance. Under the present scheme of things, under free enterprise, I do not think there is any other way to work it.
One thing, however, of which I am convinced is that as far as Canada, the government and-as far as I know-the coal board are concerned, there does not seem to be any initiative being taken by any body of government with respect to the development of our own resources. In my own end of the country the resources are there. The coal industry has a reallocation of colliery policy going back to 1926 under the old Duncan commission report, when they were shrinking the thing, centralizing the operation as far as possible, and catering to the maritime market only. That is our position today. I do not see any program for expanding the industry.
There is a program of further mechanization, with loading machines at the face, to try to increase production in the collieries that are now operating. But that is not expanding the industry, and it will not free us from almost complete dependence on the United States for our supply of coal. I was wondering if the board had anything in mind with regard to new openings in order to expand our own industry. It would not happen overnight, of course. Some planning would have to be done, keeping markets in mind. But I think it is about time that we at least began to take a long-range view with regard to developing our own resources.
I wish to read, for the minister's benefit, a passage from a letter I have here. I was surprised when I obtained this letter, and I have authority to use it. It is a letter from Mr. R. C. Vaughan, president of the Canadian National Railways, in reply to a letter from Mervyn Brown, president of Alberta Hard Coals Limited. He was writing to the president of the Canadian National Railways -and I will not read all of the letter-probing the possibilities of this resource about which we were talking last night. The pertinent part of the letter reads as follows:
In normal times the problem has been to find a market for the coal produced not only in western Canada but also coal produced in eastern Canada and the government of Canada has expended large sums of money by means of subventions to enable that to be done.
Who wrote that?

Mr. R. C. Vaughan, president of the Canadian National Railways. The letter continues:
It is quite likely that in three or four years, or sooner, that condition will again exist.
That is all of the letter that I need to quote. But it shocks me that a man in that position would make the statement that the condition which existed prior to the war with regard to the marketing of our own coal in Canada would likely be the condition with which we shall be faced within the next three or four years or sooner.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that all the talking I have done in this house about coal during the past three or four years was based on that assumption. I myself could see a drift back to what we went through after the last war when we lost the Quebec markets, and the struggle we had to get back into those markets. In the many conferences and discussions we had with the operators and with government officials in the years when our collieries were working only two or three days a week, that was always the story. They said, "You find the markets for us and we will make new openings", or "We will produce more coal", or "These collieries will operate on a five-day week basis". But it was always the question of markets. I am wondering if that kind of thought, coming from a high official of the Canadian National Railways who knows something about the field of fuel- and he must know something about it; the Canadian National Railways consume a great deal of it and haul a great deal of it across the country-is at the back of the minds of the coal board, for example, the minister himself or government officials. We are sitting back, fearful of developing our own resources in Canada, because we think that three or four years from now there may not be the markets which would permit the operation in this country. Has the board considered attempting to get away from dependence upon the United States, to the extent we are now depending upon them, by developing and extending our own resources, and trying to develop some zoning of markets in this country so as to develop the industry here?
My own opinion is, of course, as I have stated on many occasions in the house, that

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
under the system of so-called free enterprise I do not believe the coal resources of Canada will ever be developed. I do not think we shall find risk capital in this country from coast to coast, or in the central provinces, which will put money into that kind of business. I believe this resource, which is basic to our whole economic set-up, is something which will have to be managed and taken over by the government because, in my view, the government is the only organization with the necessary funds for development as it should be carried out.
I shall not discuss the matter further. My main purpose in rising was to inquire from the minister if there is any substance in the thought expressed in this letter by Mr. Vaughan, that there is a chance of our swinging back to a no-coal situation in Canada, and returning to the operation of collieries for two or three days in the week. Or has the board a program of extending and developing our own resources from a long-range standpoint, in order to get away from our dependency upon the United States to the extent which is now necessary?

I should like to follow what has been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I do so because I am deeply interested in coal, coming from a province where we have about 24 per cent of the known lignite deposits in Canada, and most of which lies in my own constituency.
I support the hon. member when he says we have to have a policy with a social consciousness at the root of it. We cannot discuss the fuel policy intelligently unless we discuss it on the basis of development across the country, not only as it applies to coal, but as it applies to oil and other fuel deposits.
I would bring to the attention of the minister the fact that it was only last year that we had a tremendous shortage of fuel in eastern Canada. During the war, too, we were dependent upon the United States for supplies of coal for our industry. I am sure that with the proper type of development in this country, and with our known deposits, we can safeguard ourselves by developing those deposits. At the present time we are imposing upon our people rigid restrictions in an attempt to save United States dollars. We must remember that we import about $150 million worth of United States coal, and pay out about $75,000,000 in freight charges to bring it to Canada, making a total of $225 million, or a quarter of our national deficit in United States dollars. This fact should bring before the government the necessity of developing our own coal fields.
In my own constituency some weeks ago one mine was shut down, and the workers in

the mine were given notice by the company that their services were no longer required because the mine was shut down indefinitely. I believe the government should take some responsibility in this regard. I am glad that the coal board has been set up, but I believe it should undertake the development of coal throughout the country, so that our nation will be safeguarded both in peace and war against any restrictions which might be placed against the importation of fuel from other countries, and so that our industries will be able to operate with the help of our own resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The purpose of the dominion fuel board is to keep informed on all problems of Canada related to fuel, and to see that no difficulties arise which may be avoided. It is the duty of the board to see that the industry functions as efficiently as possible.
There are many problems connected with fuel in Canada, the first of which is the problem of production and distribution. I can say that this problem has been handled better during the past twelve months than ever before in our history. Every mine has been kept operating at capacity, and the fuel has been sold either domestically in Canada, or in export markets. That is something which I believe was not done as well even in war years, because there were interruptions in those years which have been avoided during the past year.
Then there is the problem of supply in the central provinces. It is necessary to have sufficient coal in the country, so that no hardship results either to industry or to private citizens through a shortage of coal.
There is the further problem of fuel oil. Canada has been dependent upon outside sources for about 90 per cent of that product. I am happy to say, however, that the ratio is going to change rather rapidly, as we hope to develop in western Canada a source of supply which to a considerable extent will offset the quantities being imported at the present time.
Then there is the problem of natural gas. This is a provincial matter, because gas is not distributed outside the province in which it is produced. Nevertheless the government and the coal board have been able to give some help in western Ontario, where an effort is being made to bring in gas from Texas.
All these fuel problems require constant study. If any serious failure occurs in any of these problems, the result may be calamitous. In a country with the climate of Canada, nothing could be more serious than to be without fuel in the midst of a Canadian winter.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
Mr. MeCULLOUGH (Assiniboia): In that *connection, does not the minister think it *would be better to have a board set up which Mould take into consideration the development of all types of fuel?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
This board is charged with that responsibility. It has no mandatory powers over fuel oil, but it can be given those mandatory powers under the act, simply by the passage of an order in council.
People speak a good deal about development, and suggest that we should open new mines. The hon. member for Cape Breton South, who probably knows the problem better than I do, will agree with me that the limitation is one of manpower, the supply of qualified miners. If we had more qualified miners in western Canada we could produce more coal. If we had more workers on the face in Cape Breton we would produce more coal. The simple method of opening up new mines will not produce new miners.

Why was the apprenticeship scheme, which was established during the war in connection with the coal mines, abandoned? Miners were being developed rapidly, but that scheme was abandoned. That is why you are not getting men at the face today.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Because in wartime we had control of labour which we have lost in peacetime. My hon. friend knows how that happened.
Could this board be given that authority now?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: I am afraid not. It is impossible to order men to do anything these days. If men come forward and volunteer for apprenticeship, I am sure it could be arranged. The other matter, about which the hon. member speaks, was more or less a mandatory affair.
I am sure you would get hundreds of apprentices if you re-established the scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I shall be glad to confer with my colleague the Minister of Labour and suggest that he re-establish his school. But it Mould be a different kind of school from the one which operated during the war, as my hon. friend will appreciate.
Then, reference has been made to the lignite deposits in Saskatchewan. The hon. member knows as well as I do that lignite cannot be stored in any quantity. As the hon. member knows, the mines in Saskatche-M'an have always closed down in June, July and August since he was a small boy and probably they will in future, because the coal
must be moved from the mine into use immediately, or otherwise it will not be coal; it will be just a pile of dust. I do not know that the coal board with all its magic can do anything about that situation. An attempt has been made to briquette the coal, I think perhaps with some success. I am not sure how that briquetting process is working out.
Mr. MeCULLOUGH (Assiniboia): I do not pose as being a coal expert, but I know they are briquetting coal there and have been doing so for years. They have developed a good binder, and the briquetted coal can be shipped any place in Canada. I think the minister will admit that it is high-grade fuel in that condition.. I submit that the capacity of the briquetting plant should be increased, either by private enterprise or by the government. It would then be possible to ship the larger quantities to those parts of Canada where fuel is needed, and to sell the byproducts.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I am not familiar with the briquetting plant, but I should imagine that the mines at Estevan can produce in one day sufficient coal to keep the briquetting plant in operation for a year.
Mr. MeCULLOUGH (Assiniboia): That is true.
Then why not expand the plant?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Expand it 365 times? We must be practical about these things.
Put in a few more retorts.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The only reason the plant is operating today is that its capital cost was written off. It was sold to the present owner for one dollar. There is no great encouragement, either for the government or for anyone else, to make the capital investment required to briquette Estevan coal and expect to do the country any great good.

I was out there and had a look at that plant. The plant was set up in the first place by the Saskatchewan government, which was Liberal at that time, at a cost of $1,000,000, but it was never used. It is a low-temperature carbonization process, the process upon which Germany built her M'hole industrial set-up. There are only two of these plants in North America. This was simply a small pilot plant, and it was sold later by the government for a dollar. It is just a small affair that is struggling along.
If the coal- board took hold of it and, as suggested by the hon. member for Assiniboia, put in a few more retorts, the fuel could

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
be sent to any part of the world, once it was briquetted, and the by-products could be utilized. I suggest that there is a possibility to do something with Saskatchewan coal. The board should have a look at that plant and see what can be done about expanding it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The purpose of the coal board is to see that coal is produced as efficiently as possible in all parts of Canada; that it is distributed as efficiently as possible; that sufficient coal is brought into the deficient areas to meet their requirements; that the distribution of oil is in the best interests of Canada, and to promote the efficient production and use of fuels across the dominion. I think the board has got away to a good start.

Could the minister give us the names of the personnel of the coal board and also tell the committee if some of the members have been or are still closely connected with United States coal companies which are shipping coal into this country?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The chairman of the board is Mr. Uren, who had charge of the distribution of materials throughout the war years. Mr. D. W. Morrison was the mayor of Glace Bay. He is an old coal miner and was the unanimous choice of the miners in that area. Mr. P. Streeter is a coal operator in New Brunswick. Mr. MacLaren was associate coal controller for the dominion during the war years. He has a distributing business in Toronto and is familiar with the problems of Ontario. Mr. A. Vissac is a consulting engineer who has been operating in the western provinces for many years past. Mr. W. Whittaker is secretary of the coal association of western Canada, and Major-General Renaud is a gentleman who is familiar with the distribution problems in Quebec. He was not previously associated with the Industry.

Last evening there vas a discussion with regard to the Highwood oroperty in Alberta, and reference was made to the findings of the royal commission on coal. Has any investigation of the Highwood property been made at any time by the fuel board?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: The fuel board have received samples of the coal and have had it analysed in the dominion laboratories. There has been no opportunity to visit the property, which is not a coal operation; rather it is a coal lease. There are really two leases. My hon. friend has referred to the Highwood property. The property our friend Brown is interested in is the Burns leases, on the other side of the river.

Reference was made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South to Mr. Vaughan, president of the Canadian National Railways. When Mr. Brown, to whom reference has just been made by the minister, communicated with Mr. Vaughan in regard to the building of a branch line of some fifty miles to the Highwood property, Mr. Vaughan, among other things, said this on May 18:
The royal commission on coal, appointed by the government, in their report of December, 1946, dealt with the Highwood area (pages 37 and 38). I understand the fuel board at Ottawa has also made some investigations into those areas in relation to the general coal supply of Canada.
As the minister has just said, apparently the fuel board did not make any investigation of this area, apart from an investigation with regard to the quality of coal to be found there. I have read over the statements made last evening with regard to this matter, and it seems to me that it is rather unfair to the application which is being made to rely on the findings of the royal commission on coal. The reason for this was set out last evening by the hon. member for Calgary West when he referred to the fact that the evidence of Mr. Brown and the representations of Mr. Charles McTague, council for Mr. Brown and his associates, were not completed. Indeed, their representations were withdrawn and they themselves withdrew from the commission. That being so, I do not think the findings of the royal commission should be accepted in any way in connection with deciding upon the value of this property and the need of a spur being built.
To keep the record clear, I have in my hand a copy of a letter written by Mr. McTague. Incidentally, Mr. McTague was for some years a judge of the court of appeal of Ontario. He resigned some years ago. He is a man who would be most careful in any representations he would make, and on October 1, 1945, he wrote the following letter to Mr. J. H. Frawley.
Dear Mr. Frawley:
Re Allied Industrials Limited
With reference to your letter of September 25, and subsequent telephone conversation I have to advise that my clients wish to withdraw their applications from the commission and consequently it is not deemed necessary to file the material to which you have reference.
My clients are of the opinion after their experience at the hearing in Toronto that no good purpose will be served . . .
The reasons for that statement are set out, but I do not need to place them on the record. The letter then goes on:
Therefore, I should appreciate it if you would place on the records of the commission this letter of withdrawal.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
So far as this property is concerned, I feel that those who advocate the opening of this area do not deserve, in the interests of the country as a whole, to be met by the argument that a royal commission had met and come to a determination finally or indeed partly conclusive, because representations were not made for the reasons set out in that letter.
My hon. friend mentioned Mr. Brown, and last night certain references were made to him. I am not going to place his views before the committee, but if there was any intention on the part of the right hon. gentleman in referring to Mr. Brown as a promoter, as he did, to convey any innuendo-

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Promotion is an honourable profession, is it not?

I am glad to hear my right hon. friend say that, because it removes any suggestion that might be conveyed by the use of the words in the manner in which they were used.
Reference was made to the personnel of the coal board. I do not know anything about the members of the coal board, but it is the contention of Mr. Brown that their attitude has been far from co-operative. He points out that one of its officials was a member of the western coal association, which is unfavourable to the opening of this area. He further states that another member of the board has been the president of the Rochester and Pittsburgh Coal Company, a United States coal company, which has been exporting millions of tons of coal into Canada. He also points out that Mr. Vissac, to whom my right hon. friend referred, and who was the consulting engineer for Mr. Brown in 1944, approved the opening of the Highwood coal area. These are the representations that Mr. Brown makes, and these representations, as I see it, deserve to be answered by the minister, to the end that any sense of unfairness that is felt by Mr. Brown will be removed, if not dissipated.
My right hon. friend said in answer to the hon. member for Cape Breton South that, regardless of the properties which could be developed, lack of available miners would prevent any development. He stated that the proposal of this group with whom Mr. Brown was associated was to mine millions of tons of hard coal by strip-mining methods, thus avoiding the necessity of having underground miners. I do not know anything about this proposition from personal knowledge, but if what the Minister of Agriculture said at a dinner that I attended along with other members of this house is to be seriously regarded,
I again bring this matter to the minister's attention, to the end that further consideration be given to this application.
The minister said last night that other coal companies had built their own spur lines, but my information is that none of these spur lines has been longer than five miles or so, and in no case is there one approaching fifty miles in length. The hon. member for Davenport, who has given his usual close study to this matter says there is no spur line at all to a hard-coal mine which has been built by the operator.
One of our major responsibilities as members of this house is to see that fairness is done to all. and if the allegations and contentions of Mr. Brown be correct, then I think the whole question deserves to be reconsidered. Certainly Mr. Brown and those associated with him should not be faced with the findings of a royal commission report that was not based upon full evidence and, indeed, is based upon evidence, the representations covering which were withdrawn prior to the conclusions of the royal commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
I cannot understand what this is all about. I have read full-page advertisements attacking myself personally for something I failed to do in connection with this venture, and I have seen this group issue full-page advertisements in the press. So far as I know, Mr. Brown has never made any proposition to the government at all.
There is in the neighbourhood a mine operated by John Boyd, which is trucking its coal to the nearest railroad and getting along all right. I cannot imagine what magic there is about this particular property that requires us to build a railroad. Sixty miles is not an uneconomical trucking distance. There has been tremendous excitement and tremendous pressure about this property, but absolutely nothing done in the way of development.
Mr. Brown asked for permission to appear before the royal commission on coal, which was made up of men who had no prejudices in the matter that I know of. They heard him for a time, and then he withdrew on the advice of counsel. I would judge from that, that he did not have very much to present or that it did not carry very much weight. He applied to the Canadian National Railways. I must say that I disagree absolutely with Mr. Vaughan as to the future of the coal industry in this country; nevertheless I cannot imagine Mr. Vaughan building sixty miles of railroad into this particular property when he could build fewer miles of railroad and get an equally good product. There is no magic in this particular property. I have known about the Burns' leases since I first went to western

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
Canada thirty years ago. I have actually visited them. Probably I am the only man in the house who has evei; seen this property. What is all the shooting about? Who wants to do what? I have never been able to discover it.

I saw this man's advertisement in the paper. Naturally, as a Canadian, I was interested. I went to the Royal York hotel. I heard him contend tnany things. I said, "If you wish I will meet you in Ottawa." I made arrangements to meet him here. He never met me. I got a wire at the last moment. I told him I was willing to meet him at eleven a.m. I think the man does not know where he is heading. Why waste any more time in this House of Commons and expend many more dollars of the people's money on a man like that? The man is all talk.

I wish to refer to this matter. As a pioneer in this national fuel policy, twenty-five years ago on the 13th day of March, 1923, I introduced a resolution calling for a national fuel supply. I asked for the adoption of a policy to that end. I am too modest to call myself a Progressive; I am a Conservative. I asked for the adoption of a national policy of bonuses, subventions and subsidies, so that all the coal we use in Canada could be mined and coked under the British flag. I referred to Wales, Alberta and the maritimes. I find that the minister has made some progress. There is no doubt about it at all. We had the same difficulty when I raised this problem, on March 13, 1923. At that time we had not enough miners, no help from the national railways, no merchant marine, and all that kind of thing which we needed for the policy.
Ten years before that, we had an experiment made. In 1912 a ship left Swansea, Wales, with several thousand tons of Welsh coal and landed at the harbour improvement in my constituency, in Ashbridge's bay. One hundred and four members of parliament were down the ship channel the other day. They saw the large piles of coal, about 800,000 tons, brought in. instead of by all-rail, by water through the Welland canal from lake Erie ports; Buffalo; Erie, Pennsylvania; Ashtabula; Cleveland; and many other coal centres in Pennsylvania. We have had experiments made.
We have the same problem today. It is not a new problem at all. We knew of this problem when we started the harbour improvements. I believe the time is coming when the government should try to get more miners into the country. There are many displaced persons from Europe today who could go into the coal industry in this country. If we could get 1,000, 2,000 or 3,000 of them it would help.

Many of them have been deported from some of the mines in eastern Europe, and are now slaves working for the Russian government. If our friends at the UNO would only make some representations I believe we could get some miners into these three parts of the country.
I proposed an embargo on coal in 1923. The debate lasted three days. It is not a new problem; it has been going on since I have been in the house. It is 95 per cent a transportation problem plus a labour problem. The very same state of affairs prevails today. The same situation exists with regard to Alberta coal moving westward. We had hoped to bring in a whole lot of it. One of the western papers said they had to bring United States coal as far west as Saskatoon and other places farther up from the border, on account of Alberta coal going west. I predicted this in 1923. Hon. members will see that if they look up Hansard of March 13, 1923. It was said that the government of the day could do nothing. Five or six years before that, it was suggested that maritime coal be given bonuses, subventions and subsidies. The minister made some progress last year. I give the minister some credit for having made some progress. He should consider further the question of giving subventions to miners and mines that produce large amounts of coal.
The minister knows more about this matter than I do. I am speaking from memory. I referred to the Burns matter near Calgary at that time. They had some mines in Alberta when I brought this matter up before. I believe the government should consider the policy now along the same lines, because it is all a protectionist measure to use Canadian coal to try to save dollars. Look at what we would have saved in dollars since 1923. In 1923 we were sending out $52,000,000. We were sending that out in wages to Pennsylvania coal barons. Sir Henry Thornton was head of the Canadian National Railways at the time. He did not think very much of my policy. It would be far better for us to consider that policy and do something to develop our mines and bring them forward. Although I do not pose as a Progressive, I predicted in 1923 that the prairie provinces, which were then largely agricultural, would become, in the not too distant future, great manufacturing and mining districts. To the great credit of the Dominion of Canada, that has been proven true in the west, as the minister knows. Mining discoveries have been made. About eight or ten different types of mineral wealth have been discovered, and that is a great credit to the western natural resources of this country.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I believe a policy of some system of reasonable subventions or bonuses should be adopted to develop the mines. That policy has been adopted in some of the departments at the present time. The principle is a principle whether it is applied to coal or some other class of mineral. The provinces have applied that principle. Some of the mining areas of new Ontario have been subsidized.
Some progress has been made. I was told in 1923 that I was talking nonsense when I proposed a national hydro-electric policy for the Northwest Territories and for all Canada then. The day is not far distant when this question will be solved. It is true that in Toronto there is not as much Alberta coal as we should like to get. At the present time I believe they are down to a few hundred1 thousand tons. We have the docks at Ash-bridge's bay piled up with coal as high as the galleries. In Alberta coal they are down to two or three hundred thousand tons. We could use 500,000 tons or vastly more. That has taken place since I was the head of the harbour board. A solution of the problem is transportation, plus mining, plus deposed person's extra labour. In Alberta and the maritimes, they have the sites; they have the mines. The only trouble is transportation. The merchant marine is not doing as much as it could do in the maritimes. If we had additional miners in the country to open up the mines we could produce in Alberta and the maritimes a large part of the coal we require.
The school board is willing to take Alberta, Welsh and maritime coal. We should like to get it for our public schools. The boards of education would like to get it. Many of the businessmen would like to get it. I know that the Toronto board of trade which hon. members met the other day would like to get it. They were very glad to see my hon. friends. We hope it will be an annual visit. I see my young friend the hon. member for Fraser Valley here tonight. He is one of those who believe in the policy that I have been pressing here. We hope we shall have hon. members all back next year. If not there, at the trade fair.
I am not going to detain the committee longer tonight. We had a long day today and a long day yesterday. I want to commend the minister for the policy he has inaugurated. I hope it will be extended, so that if an ordinary citizen comes forward and gives security, either through the bank or in the way of a guarantee, the government will not lose any money.
I believe the same principle should be applied to the development of coal as the government has used in connection with housing. Money has been lent through the banks and the banks have been guaranteed. We have spent $89,000,000 in this work and the loss has amounted to only one-fifth of one per cent. We should have some such policy in connection with coal development, because next winter will be a disastrous one for the Canadian people. This has a direct bearing upon public health in Canada. I do not know what our situation will be next winter if we cannot obtain some substitutes for coal to eke out our fuel supply.
I have visited homes of soldiers, and of other people as well, in the riding I represent, and I know what conditions they are living under at the present time. In the lower part of my riding there are a great many soldiers. There are many poor families in that working men's district who are suffering severely. As a matter of fact, it might be called a soldier district. I was indeed surprised to witness the state of affairs in some of the homes I visited. There are people who are living in cellars without any fuel at all. This is a serious state of affairs. It directly affects the public health and is something that is closely related to the housing problem.
The minister is a progressive man and, during the war, he did good work. I would ask him to apply the same policy as in homes to the development of our coal mines. There is no reason why we could not make use of more displaced persons in the coal industry, and at the same time make every effort to solve the transportation problem. We should have proper cars for removing the coal. I have seen Alberta coal in transit once or twice and it was being moved in dilapidated wooden box cars. Some of the coal was falling out. It was being moved in the type of cars used before the war. There was a large vote for our national railways, and I suggest that we should have proper cars for the transportation of our coal and at the same time make use of displaced persons, where possible, as miners to aid, bringing them in for the development of the coal mining industry. If the government would introduce a proper coal policy I am sure it would receive the support of everyone. As it is, I think they have made some progress since the last session.

I have listened to the presentation by the hon. member for Calgary West and the hon. member for Davenport. I have known Mr. Brown for some time and he has always been associated with fuel enterprises. I am thinking now of the promotion of natural gas, artificial gas, peat bogs and western coal. That seems to be the latest venture.

Supply-Reconstruction and Supply
I have followed advertisements in the press and have listened to much of his propaganda with respect to this tremendous field.
I recognize that Canada is vulnerable so far as fuel is concerned, and I am inclined to think the minister is interested in finding a solution for our fuel problem. He is as much interested as any other good Canadian would be. He has no ulterior motives and he is anxious to see our resources developed. I should like to have his assurance that geologists connected with the department are acquainted with the quality and the character of the coal.
I have made inquiries, because I had something to do with the handling of Drumheller coal in western Canada. Some would slack easily and would not store over a great period of time, but if this is a rugged type of coal that could stand handling I think some method could be evolved to solve the transportation problem. This coal could be delivered to the head of the lakes, dumped in huge mounds from which it could be transshipped by water so as to get the full benefit of the water rates, which are cheaper than the rail haul.
This may have been all considered and carefully studied; but that is the thought I have in mind, because, after all, it is a transportation problem. When Alberta coal is advertised in my own city of Owen Sound and in the adjacent municipalities, people are glad to have the opportunity of using it. But, as the minister said on a previous occasion, they have not so far delivered more than 500,000 tons to the province of Ontario. Be that as it may, I still feel that if we are to consider, as we are doing at the present time, our disadvantages and disabilities in the matter of United States exchange, we can well afford to consider the advantages of subventions or otherwise in encouraging the use of our native fuel.
I do not think I have much more to say on this question. I believe that the transportation problem could be solved and that the necessary carriage facilities, the railway care, could be provided so that a great deal more coal could be delivered in Ontario. After listening to the discussion that has taken place in the committee, I do not think this is any new discovery. There is ample coal available in Alberta. They are calling it canthracite, associating it with anthracite, but it is either a lignite or a bituminous coal, as I understand. Having served on the public utilities commission in my city, I may say we bought thousands of tons of coal, and I agree with the minister that we bought our

coal without seeing the product at all. We bought it on the strength of its analysis, the B.T.U.'s and ash content. It is a free market as far as we are concerned; if Alberta coal had been available at anything like competitive prices our sympathies would have been with the Canadian product and we would have used it.
We happen to be a lake port, and my suggestion. is compatible with our own best interests. If the coal could be hauled to Fort William or Port Arthur, when grain haulage does not make a great demand upon the use of our boxcars, there is no reason why it could not be brought in. I received a good- many carloads of coal in my day, delivered in boxcars; not open dump cars. The coal could be rolled down there and piled up for water carriage, and as soon as transportation opened in the spring we could take advantage of the water.
Mr. Brown should be encouraged in his endeavours to interest capital in this venture, and our Canadian railways, both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, should have a sympathetic understanding of the situation. It is only a sixty-mile spur that is involved. I hope their purpose will not be defeated on this account. I have no quarrel with the ministry. I think they are as much concerned about this matter as we are. In the trying days of the war we valued the efforts that were made, and perhaps I should be more complimentary than critical.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: This item was passed this afternoon and we have had an hour's discussion. It is obvious that we have reached the stage where every speech is a repetition of what has been said before. Can we not pass the item and allow the Minister of External Affairs to get on with his estimates?
What I am about to say will not consist of repetition.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: There is no coal in Prince Edward Island.

I wish to make one statement. It seems that we have got down to personal matters and the personnel of the company. I think the hon. member for Simcoe North made a mistake in his reference to Mr. Brown.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext: Under what item does Mr. Brown come?
Under the same item under which this discussion has been taking place.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
There is
nothing in the item to justify the hon. member.

Supply-External Affairs

Then, as a matter of privilege may I say this? I have known Mr. Brown for years. He was one of the best citizens of our province, and he left that part of Canada as a young man. His background of parentage and training at home cannot be duplicated by any man sitting in this house. As one who listened to the hon. member for Brandon introducing him the other night, as ke knew him in the west, I can say that no one can have anything against Mr. Brown as an excellent citizen of Canada.

Let us be brief about this matter. Let us get down to business and stop wasting time. Personally I have nothing against Mr. Brown. I believe everything that has been said about Mr. Brown is quite correct. I believe no one else in Canada can equal him. But let Mr. Brown, in a businesslike manner approach the minister of reconstruction and, in a businesslike manner-with a stenographer taking down everything he says-for co-operation purposes-lay his case on the table before the proper authorities in this government. If he has anything worthwhile, he will not need to put it in the newspaper as he did and call my attention to it. I have wasted time over Mr. Brown. I waited for Mr. Brown to come to the city of Ottawa on a certain day at eleven o'clock, on the assurance that I as an independent man would lay his case before the house of parliament, and he said he was too busy to keep the appointment. I have never heard any more from the gentleman.
There is a proper channel through which to operate. This is the most important business in Canada to be discussed. Let Mr. Brown lay his case before the government of Canada. If he does not get proper attention, let Canada know the facts, and I will be one of the first to take up his brief. Otherwise, let us dispense with it tonight.
What about Mr. Jones, Mr. Smith and John Doe?

I have one question that is not about Mr. Brown. It is well known that we must import a large quantity of coal each year from the United States. It is also well known that we have a great deal of coal in Canada. We have appointed a coal board. Before this item is passed, I should like the minister to say in what way this coal board is expected to increase the production of coal in Canada next year. Exactly what is its function?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
speechtext:
The whole purpose of the board is to see that every coal miner in Canada is enabled to work as many days as he can work, to produce all the coal he can, 5849-352
and to see that the coal is marketed appropriately inside or outside Canada.

The policy the minister has outlined is a good one. With regard to what the hon. member for Beauce said not long ago, it is unfortunate that the same thing is not done in England, that the coal miners there do not work as much as they should, and that the British government does not see to it that they do. If they did that, England would be able to export coal to the value of a billion dollars more each year. Then they would need no help from any other country and there would be no dollar problem. It is socialism that is the cause of all the trouble.
Carried.
